Preface to the Tract on Response and Retribution
The Most High said: ‘Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned by man himself.’
The retribution of good and evil follows him as the shadow follows the form.
Therefore Heaven and Earth have spirits who oversee transgressions, and according to the lightness or gravity of a man’s offenses they take away from his tally of days.
When his tally is diminished, he grows poor and wasteful, and meets with many sorrows.
All men detest him.
Punishment and calamity follow after him.
Auspicious blessings shun him.
Evil stars bring disaster upon him.
When his tally is exhausted, he dies.

There are also the Spirit Lords of the Three Terraces and the Northern Dipper, who hover above a man’s head, record his sins and evils, and take away from his measure of years (ji, twelve years) and his tally of days (suan).
There are also the three corpse-spirits, which dwell within a man’s body. On every gengshen day they ascend to the heavenly bureaus and report his offenses.
On the last day of the lunar month, the Stove God does the same.
Whenever a man commits an offense, a grave one costs him a ji, twelve years; a light one costs him a suan, a hundred days.
Such offenses, great and small, number several hundred; one who seeks long life must first avoid them.
If it accords with the Way, advance; if it does not accord with the Way, withdraw.
Do not tread the crooked byways; do not deceive in the darkened chamber.
Accumulate virtue and pile up merit.
Cherish all beings with a compassionate heart.
Loyalty and filial devotion.

The more advanced technology becomes, the more the human heart goes astray; the more refined material civilization becomes, the more morality decays; the more the mind is defiled, the worse public order becomes. How, after all, can the world and the hearts of men be saved? How can crime be reduced? How can one seek blessings for oneself? How can one avert disaster and escape calamity? And how, above all, can there be peace in the nation and contentment among the people, timely wind and rain, an end to war forever, and peace under heaven? I believe these are the questions that modern people care about most, and worry over most.

Yet for all this care and worry, our efforts to resolve the world’s disorders, its natural disasters and man-made calamities, seem to accomplish very little; matters even go from bad to worse, and the problems grow more serious by the day. The result of people seeking blessings for themselves has often turned instead into seeking calamities for themselves. The root of it all is that modern people are too superstitious about science: their understanding of the standard of good and evil and of the principle of karmic retribution is not clear enough — indeed, they misunderstand it deeply. Acting in opposition to these truths, they naturally fail to obtain blessings and instead invite disaster and bitter fruit. This is the fundamental reason for the corruption of the human heart, the soaring of crime, and the great disorder of the world!

The book Compilation of the Tract on Response and Retribution is broad and profound. It gathers up the highest principle that blessings attend the auspicious and calamities the perverse, that goodness is repaid with blessing and licentiousness with disaster, and gives it forth in arguments that shake heaven and earth and startle the eye and mind. As to what is good and what is evil, what good reward follows doing good, and what evil reward follows doing evil — it perceives and illumines their roots with perfect clarity, so that after reading it one thoroughly understands the principles of good and evil, cause and effect, calamity and blessing, and knows that selfishness and self-interest in fact lose the great benefit and win the great calamity. Thus everyone spurs himself on to do good, hoping thereby to gather blessings and avert disaster. Hence this book’s benefit to the world and to men’s hearts is exceedingly deep and far-reaching. In the Qing dynasty, Minister Peng Ningzhi inscribed it as ‘a book the prime minister must read,’ and added: ‘It is not that having read this book one may become a top graduate or a prime minister; it is that a top graduate or a prime minister absolutely must not fail to read it.’ Minister Peng’s words may be called thoroughly penetrating. Master Yinguang said: ‘Judged by its utmost reach, this book stops at attaining immortality; but if one practices it with the great bodhi mind, one can transcend the ordinary and enter the sage, escape birth and death, and perfectly accomplish the Buddha Way.’ Master Yinguang, throughout his life, spared no effort in spreading this book. Elder Master Jingkong went further, urging Buddhist disciples to read, recite, receive, and uphold this book as they would the precepts, and he bestowed on it the name The Way of Gathering Blessings and Averting Disaster. All of these rest on profoundly deep reasons.

Deeply awed by the principle that ‘all dharmas are empty, but cause and effect are not empty,’ this society devotes its full strength to spreading the teaching of cause and effect for the transformation of men’s hearts. The earlier compilation of Liaofan’s Four Lessons and the present translation of the condensed vernacular edition of the Compilation are expressions of this same ideal. Here we thank our society’s teacher, Elder Master Jingkong, for his encouragement and urging; Upasaka Zheng for his long and patient guidance of the translation work; Upasaka Zhong for proposing the project, polishing the writing, and proofreading; and Upasaka Ruan and several professors for their help in checking the source materials — all of which allowed this book to be completed smoothly and to benefit all quarters. It is our earnest hope that everyone who reads this book will deeply believe in cause and effect and strive to cut off evil and cultivate good. Once such a custom takes hold, courtesy and yielding will flourish, calamity and warfare will cease forever, the people will be peaceful and happy, and the world will be at peace!
January 25, 2000 CE
Preface written at the Liaofan Dharma Propagation Society

Although the Tract on Response and Retribution comes from the Daoist canon, the annotations in the Compilation mostly cite Confucian books and Buddhist sutras; so that reading one book yields the essential meaning of the three teachings — truly the first thing to rejoice over! The Compilation gathers the various annotated editions of ancient and modern times and, after careful examination and selection, refining and refining again, was edited into a book; so that reading the Compilation is equal to having read every annotated edition of the Tract — truly the second thing to rejoice over! The editor’s eye and hand were incomparably brilliant, and the reader who gains such a good guide will thereby broaden his mind and plant a wide field of blessed conditions — truly the third thing to rejoice over! The loftiest maxims of Confucianism, its labor of making the will sincere and the heart upright, its essential keys to cultivating the self and regulating the family: more than half of these are already included in the Compilation. The literary prajñā of the Buddhist gate may also be glimpsed in this book, and the essential principles of the Daoist discipline of the mind are likewise gathered in the Compilation — truly the fourth thing to rejoice over! Therefore the Compilation is not merely the king of annotations on the Tract; it is truly the king of all good books!

Whoever is able to see this book is a person of blessing. If one can read it straight through to the end, still the thoughts and quiet the mind, chew and savor it over and over, and take its principles to heart; and if one then earnestly puts them into practice — such a one is a person of great blessing! If one can go further still, refining and refining again, then the principles by which one becomes a sage or a worthy, a Buddha or a patriarch, all lie within this book! If one lives in the world and cannot meet this king of books, then one will sink through long kalpas and find it very hard to escape the wheel of rebirth — is that not a great misfortune? Moreover, the annotations of the Tract are so clear, so detailed, so penetrating, so earnest — not merely instructing one at one’s ear, not merely crying out aloud, but with a heart of compassion for heaven and pity for men, one may say, speaking through tears. Therefore those who have the good fortune to read this book should naturally turn back at once — what is there to hesitate or doubt?

The people whose evil retribution is recorded in the Compilation hasten toward death like wild ducks, and even at the very moment of death they cannot awaken. This is all because in their whole lives they never had the chance to read the Tract on Response and Retribution! Thus the benefit the Tract brings to human life is not only the one shortcut for turning calamity into blessing; it is the single gateway for transcending the ordinary and entering the sage! May everyone read it with care.
The Most High’s Tract on Response and Retribution
The Most High said: ‘Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned by man himself. The retribution of good and evil follows him as the shadow follows the form.’

Therefore Heaven and Earth have spirits who oversee transgressions, and according to the lightness or gravity of a man’s offenses they take away from his tally of days. When the tally is diminished, he grows poor and wasteful, meets with many sorrows, and all men detest him; punishment and calamity follow after him, auspicious blessings shun him, and evil stars bring disaster upon him. When his tally is exhausted, he dies.

There are also the Spirit Lords of the Three Terraces and the Northern Dipper, who hover above a man’s head, record his sins and evils, and take away from his measure of years and his tally of days. There are also the three corpse-spirits, which dwell within a man’s body. On every gengshen day they ascend to the heavenly bureaus and report his offenses. On the last day of the lunar month, the Stove God does the same. Whenever a man commits an offense, a grave one costs him a ji, a light one a suan. Such offenses, great and small, number several hundred; one who seeks long life must first avoid them.

If it accords with the Way, advance; if it does not accord with the Way, withdraw. Do not tread the crooked byways; do not deceive in the darkened chamber. Accumulate virtue and pile up merit; cherish all beings with a compassionate heart. Be loyal and filial, friendly and fraternal; rectify yourself and transform others. Pity the orphan and succor the widow; honor the aged and cherish the young. Even insects, grasses, and trees must not be injured. One should grieve over others’ misfortunes and rejoice in others’ goodness. Relieve others in urgency and rescue them in danger. Regard another’s gain as your own gain; regard another’s loss as your own loss. Do not publish others’ faults; do not display your own strengths. Check evil and promote good; yield the greater share and take the lesser. Bear insult without resentment; receive favor as though startled. Bestow kindness without seeking reward; give to others without regret.

As for the good man, all men respect him, the heavenly Way protects him, blessings and emoluments follow him, all evil influences keep far from him, and the spirits guard him. Whatever he undertakes must succeed, and immortality may be hoped for. One who seeks to be a celestial immortal should establish one thousand three hundred good deeds; one who seeks to be an earthly immortal should establish three hundred good deeds.

But if one acts without righteousness and walks against reason; if one takes evil for ability and hardens his heart to do harm; if one secretly injures the good and virtuous, and covertly insults ruler and parents; if one treats his teachers with disrespect and betrays those he serves; if one deceives the ignorant and slanders his fellow students; if one is false, accusing, and fraudulent, and attacks his own clan and kin; if one is stubborn and unkind, cruel and self-willed; if one judges right and wrong improperly and takes sides perversely; if one oppresses subordinates to win merit and flatters superiors to court their favor; if one receives kindness without gratitude and broods on grievances without end —

If one holds the people of Heaven in contempt and throws the government of the state into disorder; if one rewards the unrighteous and punishes the innocent; if one kills men to take their wealth and overturns others to seize their place; if one slaughters those who surrender and slays those who submit; if one demeans the upright and pushes aside the worthy; if one bullies the orphan and oppresses the widow; if one casts aside the law and takes bribes; if one calls the straight crooked and the crooked straight; if one makes light matters heavy and adds anger to those already condemned; if one knows his fault and does not mend it, and knows the good and does not do it; if one shifts his own guilt onto others and blocks the arts and skills of others; if one reviles and slanders the sages and worthies, and encroaches upon the Way and its virtue —

If one shoots birds in flight and hunts running beasts; if one digs out hibernating creatures and startles roosting birds; if one fills up burrows and overturns nests, injures the unborn and breaks eggs; if one wishes others to fail and ruins others’ success; if one endangers others to secure himself and diminishes others to benefit himself; if one exchanges evil for good and for private ends sets aside the public; if one steals others’ abilities and hides others’ virtues; if one exposes others’ ugliness and denounces their private affairs; if one wastes others’ goods and wealth and separates kin from kin; if one encroaches on what others love and helps others do wrong; if one gives free rein to his will and puts on airs, shaming others to win; if one ruins others’ crops and breaks up others’ marriages —

If one is rich and arrogant, or escapes by luck yet knows no shame; if one claims credit for kindness and shifts blame for faults, shifting disaster onto others and selling evil; if one buys empty reputation and harbors a treacherous heart; if one thwarts others’ strengths and shields his own weaknesses; if one uses power to coerce and threaten, and gives rein to violence, killing and wounding; if one cuts and tailors without cause, and butchers and cooks without propriety; if one scatters and wastes the five grains and troubles the multitude of living beings; if one destroys others’ households to take their wealth and treasures; if one breaches dikes and sets fires to harm people’s dwellings; if one throws order into confusion to ruin others’ work; if one damages others’ implements and vessels to cut off their use —

When he sees another honored and noble, he wishes him exiled and demoted. When he sees another wealthy, he wishes him ruined and scattered. When he sees another’s beauty, he rouses a lustful mind. When he owes another goods or money, he wishes him dead. When his requests are not granted, he gives way to cursing and hatred. When he sees another’s misfortune, he speaks of his faults. When he sees another’s body or appearance deformed, he laughs at him; when he sees another’s talent worthy of praise, he suppresses it.

If one buries charms and works sorcery to harm others, or uses poison to kill trees; if one is angry with one’s teachers and offends one’s father and elder brothers; if one takes by force and extorts, delighting in encroachment and seizure; if one plunders and loots to grow rich, and schemes craftily to gain promotion; if one rewards and punishes unfairly and indulges in pleasure beyond measure; if one is harsh and cruel to subordinates and intimidates others; if one resents Heaven and blames men, and curses the wind and reviles the rain; if one sets men to fighting and litigation, and recklessly pursues factions and cliques; if one follows the words of wife and concubines and disobeys the teachings of father and mother; if one forgets the old when he gains the new, and says one thing while his heart means another; if one is greedy for wealth and deceives his superiors; if one fabricates evil words and slanders and destroys the innocent; if one defames others and calls it uprightness, and reviles the gods and calls it correctness; if one abandons the obedient and imitates the rebellious, and turns from kin to strangers; if one calls heaven and earth to witness his petty grudges, and summons the spirits to attest his base affairs —

If one gives and then regrets it, and borrows and does not repay; if one seeks beyond his portion and contrives by force to gain; if one indulges lust to excess, harboring poison in his heart while wearing a kindly face; if one feeds others with filthy food and deludes the crowd with heterodox ways; if one uses short measures and narrow rules, light scales and small pints; if one mixes the false with the true to reap wicked profit; if one presses the good into lowliness and cheats the foolish; if one is insatiably greedy and curses and swears to win his case —

If one is addicted to wine and disorderly, and kindred quarrel and contend; if men are not loyal and good, and women are not gentle and obedient; if one does not live in harmony with his wife, and she does not respect her husband; if one is ever fond of boasting and given to jealousy; if one behaves without decency toward wife and children, and without propriety toward parents-in-law; if one slights the spirits of the departed and disobeys the commands of superiors; if one does what is of no benefit and harbors a heart turned outward; if one curses himself and curses others, and shows partial hatred and partial love; if one crosses over wells and stoves, and leaps over food and over people; if one injures children and procures abortions, and practices much that is secret and devious; if one sings and dances on the last day of the month and at the winter sacrifice, and wails and rages on the first morning of the month; if one spits, blows his nose, or urinates facing north, and chants or weeps facing the stove; if one lights incense with the stove fire and cooks food with filthy firewood; if one rises at night and goes about naked, and carries out executions on the eight seasonal festivals; if one spits at shooting stars and points at rainbows; if one recklessly points at the three luminaries and stares long at the sun and moon; if in the spring months one burns the fields for hunting; if one reviles and curses facing north; if without cause one kills turtles and beats snakes.

For sins such as these, the Master of Destinies takes away a man’s ji or suan according to their lightness or gravity. When his tally is exhausted, he dies. If guilt remains after death, then calamity reaches his descendants.

Again, for those who seize the wealth of others by force, the reckoning is made against their wives, children, and household, until they come gradually to death and loss. If they do not die, then fire, flood, robbers, lost or destroyed goods, illness, and slanderous tongues — all such things — are made to pay the value of what was wrongly taken.

Again, he who kills a man unjustly is but exchanging weapons to kill himself. He who takes wealth unrighteously is like one who saves his hunger with tainted meat or slakes his thirst with poisoned wine: he is not without a brief surfeit, but death comes with it.

When the heart gives rise to good, though the good be not yet done, auspicious spirits already follow him. When the heart gives rise to evil, though the evil be not yet done, baleful spirits already follow him. If one who has done evil afterward repents and reforms, does no evil at all and practices every good, in time he will surely obtain auspicious blessings — this is what is meant by turning calamity into blessing. Therefore the auspicious man speaks good, looks good, and does good: three goods in one day, and in three years Heaven will surely send down blessings upon him. The baleful man speaks evil, looks evil, and does evil: three evils in one day, and in three years Heaven will surely send down calamities upon him. Why then do you not strive to practice it?
Dictated by the Emperor Lord Wenchang)

The Emperor Lord Wenchang said: ‘For seventeen lives I have borne the body of a scholar-official, and never once did I oppress the people or deal cruelly with my subordinates. I relieved men in their urgency, succored them in their want, bore with their faults, and pitied them in their orphaned state. With my whole heart I did thus, submitting myself to the decrees of Heaven; therefore I have long since realized the true rank.’

The Emperor Lord Wenchang said: ‘Through seventeen lives I have always borne the body of a scholar-official, and never once did I oppress the people or treat my subordinates with cruelty. I relieved men in their distress and succored them in their poverty; I bore with men’s faults and pitied men’s loneliness. With a single heart I did thus, advancing without slackening, submitting to the arrangements of Heaven; practicing this for long, I was able to realize the rank of Perfected Lord.’

[Emperor Lord Wenchang] is also called “Emperor Wenchang” or “Lord Wenchang.” The Emperor Lord Wenchang is the deity honored by folk religion and Daoism as the one who governs the official rank, salary, and success of scholars. “Wenchang” was originally the name of a constellation, also called the Wenchang Star or the Literary Star, the star that presides over literary fortune and examination success.
[Zhenjun]
In Daoism, those who attain the Way and become immortals are called Perfected Ones (zhenren); of these, the highest are called zhenjun, Perfected Lords.
Now I exhort the people of the world to recite the Most High’s Tract on Response and Retribution once each day, and to practice in accordance with it; and also to write out one copy (zhi)

, to gaze upon morning and evening and practice accordingly. Practice it for two years, and ten thousand sins are dissolved; practice it for four years, and a hundred blessings all gather; practice it for seven years, and your sons and grandsons will be worthy and wise, gloriously ascending the examination ranks; practice it for ten years, and your lifespan will be lengthened; practice it for fifteen years, and all things will go as you wish; practice it for twenty years, and your sons and grandsons will become ministers and councilors; practice it for thirty years, and your name will be inscribed in the register of immortals; practice it for fifty years, and the gods of Heaven will revere you, and your name will be ranked among the immortal host.

Now I exhort the people of the world to recite the Most High’s Tract on Response and Retribution once each day and to cultivate practice in accordance with it; and also to write out one copy, to gaze upon it reverently day and night, and to practice accordingly. Practice it for two years, and ten thousand sins are dissolved; practice it for four years, and a hundred blessings all gather; practice it for seven years, and your sons and grandsons will be worthy and wise and gloriously pass the presented-scholar examination; practice it for ten years, and your lifespan will be lengthened; practice it for fifteen years, and all things will go as you wish; practice it for twenty years, and your sons and grandsons will become ministers and councilors; practice it for thirty years, and your name will be recorded in the register of immortals; practice it for fifty years, and the gods of Heaven will revere you, and you will accomplish the state of immortality.

Not to apply the mind to such practice, but to do and then stop, practicing today and abandoning tomorrow; when human affairs go awry, the field of the heart grows daily darker; though the scripture be recited by mouth, the heart does not awaken — this is to profane Heaven, a sin that admits no pardon.

Not to follow the teachings of the Most High’s Tract on Response and Retribution and strive in practice, but to do and then stop, practicing today and abandoning tomorrow; in one’s dealings with others, to violate the principles set forth and the deeds listed in the Tract — so that human affairs go awry — the field of the heart grows daily darker, and though the mouth recites the scripture, the heart does not awaken: this is to profane Heaven, a sin that admits no pardon.

chuò
to cease, to stop midway.
Annotated, Explained, Attested, and Illustrated: The Condensed Vernacular Edition of the Compilation of the Most High’s Tract on Response and Retribution, Volume One
[Explanation]
The Most High Lord Lao said: ‘A man’s calamity and fortune have no fixed gate at all; they are entirely summoned by himself!’
[Analysis]

The Most High is the Most High Lord Lao, surnamed Li and named Er, styled Boyang — that is, Laozi, the sage of the Zhou dynasty. After he attained the Way and became an immortal, he proclaimed the teaching of Heaven and founded the Daoist religion, and he is the supremely honored sage of Heaven. The Tract on Response and Retribution is the book in which the Most High teaches the people of the world to reform evil and practice good. Gan, response, means to summon by influence; ying, retribution, means the recompense. It tells people that if they summon causes by good or evil, they will surely receive the fruit of calamity or blessing sent down by Heaven. As it is said, where there is a summons there must be a response, and the response follows immediately upon the summons. This serves to make manifest the principle that the Way of Heaven returns what it receives, and to awaken in the people of the world a heart of reverence and awe: knowing that doing evil must bring the evil retribution of disaster, illness, and early death, their hearts are afraid and they dare not do it; knowing that doing good must bring the good retribution of blessing, long life, and celestial immortality, their hearts desire it and they bravely do it. Therefore the chapter is titled Response and Retribution.

‘Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned by man himself. The retribution of good and evil follows him as the shadow follows the form.’ These four sentences are the general guiding principle of the whole chapter, and the very purpose of the Most High’s instruction. As for the mind of the sage and worthy, it is not that he first seeks blessings and avoids calamity and only then cuts off evil and practices good. As for the principle of creation, so long as one accumulates good, blessings will surely shade his descendants; and if one accumulates evil, calamity will surely extend to his descendants. This is precisely the principle stated in the Book of Changes: ‘The family that accumulates good will surely have abundant blessings; the family that accumulates evil will surely have abundant calamities’ — and there is never the slightest error in it.

‘Summoned by himself’ means called forth by oneself; as it is said, what one does, one himself receives. You should know that Heaven and Earth have no selfish partiality, and that good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing, are all summoned by a man’s own mind. Yet before a thought arises in a man, this mind is pure and still, like empty space — where in it could good or evil be? Only because a thought first stirs: if it turns toward what is good, that is good; if it turns toward what is bad, that is evil. In the beginning it is no more than one thought arising and one deed done; but afterward, as days and months accumulate, there comes to be the difference between a good man and an evil man. Therefore whether a man meets calamity or blessing is decided entirely at the moment when the thought of good or evil first arises. Hence the Most High opens by saying: ‘Calamity and fortune have no gate; they are summoned by man himself.’ This is to warn the people of the world to watch carefully over the arising of their thoughts. If there is the slightest error in this, then the retribution of calamity or blessing will be as far apart as heaven and earth.
Story One:

Chan Master Lingyuan of the Song dynasty said to Mr. Yichuan: ‘Calamity can give birth to blessing, and blessing can give birth to calamity. The reason calamity can give birth to blessing is that when a man is in danger or disaster, he earnestly seeks peace and is able to comprehend deeply the principle of obtaining peace; above all, he can hold fear and reverence in his heart and be careful in his words and deeds. The reason blessing can give birth to calamity is that when a man dwells in safety, he cannot think of danger; moreover he gives free rein to thoughts of extravagance and pleasure, his words and conduct are proud and lax, and above all he often acts rashly and arrogantly, even to the point of mistreating others.’
Story Two:

Zhang Zi (Mr. Zhang Hengqu) of the Song dynasty said: ‘The beginning of rectifying the mind should be to take one’s own mind as a strict teacher. Whenever one is about to act, one will know to be careful, cautious, and vigilant with oneself. Practice this way for one or two years, and so long as one can hold to it earnestly and firmly, the mind will of itself become rectified.’
Story Three:

The old monk of Zhenkong Temple once said: ‘The idle thoughts of ordinary people are never fixed. Perhaps one recalls the honors and disgraces, the kindnesses and enmities, the sorrows and joys, the partings and reunions of several decades past, along with all sorts of idle feelings — these are the idle thoughts of the past. Or perhaps a matter has come before one and may be undertaken, yet in the heart one shrinks back, hesitating and unable to decide — these are the idle thoughts of the present. Or perhaps one looks forward to future glory, wealth, and honor, to the advancement of one’s sons and grandsons, and to all manner of things that are by no means certain to succeed or be obtained — these are the idle thoughts of the future.’ These three kinds of idle thoughts, whether they arise or cease, we call the deluded mind. If one can simply see through them as deluded, and the moment a deluded thought arises cut it off on the spot, this is called the awakened mind. Therefore it is said: ‘Do not fear the arising of deluded thoughts; fear only that you become aware too late.’ If this mind is pure and still like empty space, then affliction has no place to stand!
Story Four:

Mr. Zhao Kangjing of the Song dynasty once used a bottle, black beans, and white beans to practice the work of the mind. Whenever a good thought arose, he would drop a white bean into the bottle; whenever an evil thought arose, he would drop a black bean into the bottle. When he first began, the black beans he dropped in were many; afterward they gradually grew fewer. In the course of time he forgot even the two kinds of thoughts, good and evil, and entered the state of ‘not thinking of good, not thinking of evil,’ with no miscellaneous thoughts in the mind; in the end he discarded the bottle and the beans and had no further use for them.
Story Five:

During the Song dynasty, Wei Zhongda held office in the Hanlin Academy. Once the ghost-soldiers led his soul down to the underworld. The chief judge of the underworld ordered the clerks under him to bring up the two registers of the good and evil deeds he had done in the world of the living. When the registers were brought and examined, his register of evil deeds was so great that it spread over an entire courtyard; while the register of good deeds was no bigger than a single chopstick. The chief judge then ordered a scale brought to weigh them, and the evil register that filled the courtyard was in fact the lighter, while the tiny roll of good deeds no bigger than a chopstick was the heavier. Wei Zhongda asked: ‘I am not yet forty years old — how could I have committed so many faults and sins?’ The chief judge said: ‘So long as a single thought is not upright, that is a sin; there is no need to wait until you actually commit it. For example, when you saw a woman’s beauty and a bad thought stirred, that was already an offense.’ Wei Zhongda then asked what was recorded in the register of good deeds. The chief judge said: ‘Once the emperor wished to undertake a great project, to build a stone bridge at Mount San. You submitted a memorial urging the emperor not to build it, so as to spare the people toil and the treasury expense — this is the draft of your memorial.’ Wei Zhongda said: ‘I did speak of it, but the emperor did not listen and the work went forward anyway; it had no effect on the conduct of that affair. How can this memorial still have such great power?’ The chief judge said: ‘Though the emperor did not heed your advice, your thought was utterly sincere, and its purpose was to spare millions of common people from labor service. Had the emperor listened to you, your merit would have been even greater! If you were willing to use this same mind to save the people of the world, that would not be difficult either. It is a pity that your evil thoughts were so many that the power of your good was reduced by half, and there is no hope of your official rank rising to prime minister.’ Afterward Wei Zhongda did serve as an official, and indeed he rose only to be Minister of Personnel, and never became prime minister.
[Further Analysis]

What a pity! Zhongda’s evil consisted only of empty evil thoughts, which he never carried out, and still it cut down the blessings of his present life; while Zhongda’s good consisted only of empty words that the emperor never adopted, and yet the power of that good actually outweighed the register of evil that filled the whole courtyard! From this example we know that if good or evil deeds are actually done, the power of that good or evil is even greater. It is evident that the place where a thought first stirs is the very gate of calamity and blessing!
[Excellent Words]

‘Doing good is like the grass of a spring garden: you do not see it grow, yet it increases day by day. Doing evil is like a whetstone: you do not see it wear, yet it diminishes day by day.’ So calamity and blessing shift and increase or decrease without our knowing it; one who has no wisdom finds it hard to perceive.

Chan Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch of the Tang dynasty, said: ‘All fields of blessing are not apart from a single square inch of the heart.’ The Buddhist scriptures also say: ‘Good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing, are all created by the mind.’
The retribution of good and evil is like the shadow following the body: wherever the man goes, the shadow follows him there, and the two are never parted!

Good and evil are spoken of with respect to the human mind, while retribution is spoken of with respect to the principle of Heaven. You should know that when the body stands straight, the shadow is straight too; when the body leans, the shadow leans too — there is never the slightest deviation. So too, planting a good cause must bring a joyful retribution, and planting an evil cause must bring a painful retribution. The sages have explained these principles in great detail, yet it is a pity that ordinary people without wisdom do not believe them, and so turn their backs on good and face toward evil. For they see that some who do good now have very rough fates, while some who do evil not only live long but are very rich and honored; and the various retributions received in this life are all different. So they say: ‘Good and evil do not seem to be requited after all, and cause and effect seem hardly credible.’ This is because these foolish people without wisdom do not know that in this world there are no men who live to be several hundred years old, and that Heaven has no cases that are closed immediately. Since there are very few people in this world who are purely good or purely evil, the opportunities to do good or to do evil are also the most numerous. Because thoughts may shift, retribution must be weighed with care. It may be requited on one’s own person, or on one’s sons and grandsons; it may be requited in this life, or in a later life; it may be great or small, swift or slow — though there may be changes and shifts within it, there is never the slightest error. As the common saying goes: ‘Good and evil will be requited in the end; the only question is whether it comes early or late.’ And: ‘It is not that there is no requital; the time has not yet come.’ So do not look only at the present; you should look to the final outcome. For the retribution of good and evil is surely as the shadow follows the form!

According to the Buddhist scriptures, karmic retribution must be discussed in terms of three lifetimes. The first is retribution in this life, that is, receiving the fruit in this very life. The second is retribution in the next life, that is, receiving the fruit only in the second life. The third is retribution in later lives, that is, receiving the fruit in the third life, or in the tenth, hundredth, thousandth, or ten-thousandth life. Therefore one who does good in this life and yet meets with disaster is receiving the ripening of the evil karma made in a former life. And one who does evil in this life and yet receives blessings is receiving the ripening of the good karma made in a former life. So it is that within blessing there is calamity, and within calamity there is blessing — precisely because one is not purely good or purely evil. That blessings come at first and calamity at the end is because his good heart has retreated. That calamity comes at first and blessing at the end is because his evil heart has repented. If the retribution of the pain and joy of the good and evil he has done undergoes no change, this shows a direct retribution. If calamity and auspiciousness appear alternately, this shows how subtle and wondrous retribution is. And there are further the hidden virtues and hidden evils that men cannot see, which are retributions beyond what men’s ears and eyes can hear and see.

You should know that the laws of this world of ours still have omissions and gaps, but the Way of Heaven’s retribution for good and evil is absolutely free from any risk of oversight. Therefore it is said: ‘Do good and do evil, and retribution follows like a shadow; do not say that doing evil goes unrequited — simply wait until the evil is full to the brim. Do not say that cultivating good has no response — simply wait until the good fruit is perfectly ripe.’ The Buddhist scriptures also say: ‘Though a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has made does not perish; when causes and conditions meet, the fruit of retribution is still received by oneself.’ From this we know that the pain and joy we receive within the three realms, and our rising into the three good paths or sinking into the three evil paths within the six realms of rebirth, are all summoned by our own minds. You should know that the net of Heaven is hard to escape: even if one wishes to flee, it is like a traveler meeting a great rain on the road — look in all four directions and everything is dripping wet, with nowhere at all to shelter from the rain. Yet most people in the world do not awaken and cannot see through to the truth of cause, condition, and retribution. If the retribution lies far off, of course they cannot see it; and even retribution that is visible they mostly take as ordinary good or bad circumstances and pay it no attention. Being thus careless in ordinary times and unable to perceive, when they meet with some great auspicious or great inauspicious fact that ought to be believed, they instead bring out a few cases that did not come true and use them to deny it. Thus they delude themselves and doubt themselves. Even one of long experience in life, who suddenly awakens to some principle, by then is already old and his habits are already formed, hard to change. And the young, whose high spirits are at their peak, find it even harder to believe. This is why so many people in the world lose themselves and walk into byways — how sad!

In Chongming of the Qing dynasty there was a man named Huang Yongjue. A physiognomist once cast his fortune for him and said he could live only to sixty. Later a ship from the southern seas met a great wind and was about to capsize; Huang Yongjue quickly brought out ten taels of gold and bought a fishing boat to go to the rescue, saving thirteen lives in all. Afterward he met that physiognomist again, and this time the physiognomist looked at Huang Yongjue in great astonishment and said: ‘Mr. Huang, your whole face is marked with the lines of hidden virtue! You must have accumulated great virtue and done great good. Not only will you have a son, but your son will pass the examinations, and you will live to a great age.’ Afterward Huang Yongjue indeed had a son named Huang Zhenfeng, who took first place in the metropolitan examination in the jiwei year of the Kangxi reign; and Huang Yongjue lived to more than ninety and obtained a peaceful end. From this we know that the Way of Heaven is utterly true and trustworthy — why will people not forsake evil and do good?

In Xiushui there was a man named Tu Panqi, who in ordinary life did every kind of evil: he taught people to fight and go to law, seized others’ property by force, and violated other men’s wives and daughters; and whenever things went against his wishes, he would point at heaven and curse the earth, and call down maledictions on the gods. One day Tu Panqi suddenly dropped dead; only after a whole night did he revive. And he called his wife to gather everyone together and speak, saying: ‘The King of the Underworld says: the living in the world of the light do not know the retributive pain suffered by the dead in the underworld! And to feel that pain only after the retribution has come is already too late. What is pitiable is that many people in the world of the light do not know how dreadful it is and still strive desperately to do evil! Today Tu Panqi may be called a man of monstrous guilt, and so I have borrowed you to warn the people of the world.’ Having said this, Tu Panqi took a knife and cut off his own genitals, saying: ‘This is the retribution for licentiousness.’ Then he gouged out his own eyes, saying: ‘This is the retribution for glaring in anger at the immortals and Buddhas, at my parents, and at living beings.’ Then he chopped off his hands, saying: ‘This is the retribution for slaughtering living creatures!’ Then he cut open his belly and dug out his heart, saying: ‘This is the retribution for a sinister and cruel heart.’ Then he cut out his tongue, saying: ‘This is the retribution for deceitful speech and evil words.’ The neighbors all came running to look, and not one was not seized with dread. Tu Panqi lingered on like this for six days and died with no whole skin left on his body. This is what is meant by doing it oneself and receiving it oneself — and the retribution was as swift as this!
[Conclusion]

At the Eastern Peak Temple there is a couplet that says: ‘The villains of the world of light — ruthlessly they wrong their own hearts and defy reason. The retribution of the underworld — from ancient times to now, whom has it ever let pass?’ Why must people sin with their eyes open and bring endless suffering upon themselves?

For in a man’s life, whether by day or by night, at every moment, above and below and on all four sides, there are spirits who preside over men’s offenses and transgressions, watching and examining; and according to the lightness or gravity of the offenses each man commits, they take away from his tally of years. (A hundred days of life is called one suan. For a light offense a lesser amount is taken; for a grave one, a greater.)

In Heaven there are the Three Officials and the Five Emperors, and a hundred spirits and various bureaus; on earth there are the Five Sacred Peaks, the Four Great Rivers, the City Gods, and the local earth gods. There is also the Department of Rising Thoughts, which makes a special record of the good and evil of men’s arising thoughts. All of these are what are called the spirits who oversee transgressions. Now the heart of Heaven is compassionate and benevolent, and it wishes the people of the world to do good and put away evil in the place that only they themselves know within their own hearts; therefore the spirits who oversee transgressions exist, to examine the evil deeds men commit, to measure their lightness or gravity, and to deduct a hundred days from a man’s lifespan. Hence it is said: ‘The whispered words of men sound in Heaven like thunder! If a man does something against his conscience in a dark room, he absolutely cannot escape the spirits’ eyes, sharp as lightning.’ The Book of Songs and the Book of Documents also say: ‘God watches day and night over the deeds done by every person in the world through body, speech, and mind.’ This is the principle of what is called the ten eyes watching, the ten hands pointing, and the spirits hearing. If one understands this principle, then in the place that only one’s own heart knows there are naturally spirits and ghosts, stricter in their scrutiny than the visible spirits of heaven and earth — this is what is meant by the unity of Heaven and man.

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘After each person is born, two heavenly beings follow him, one named Tong Sheng, Same Birth, and the other named Tong Ming, Same Name. These two heavenly beings can always see the words and deeds of the person they follow; but the person followed by the heavenly beings cannot see them.’ These two heavenly beings are what are called the two youths of good and evil, and every hour of the twenty-four they record a man’s good and evil words and deeds, including the deeds of his mind. Therefore in all our arising thoughts, our speech and conduct, our dealings with others and reception of things, we should constantly bear in mind that these two heavenly beings are watching and recording at every time and in every place, and we should not let our evil thoughts continue unbroken. If by chance an evil thought arises, we must at once become aware of it and turn it around. Therefore in mastering oneself, one must first master where mastery is hardest, tracing all the way to the place where thoughts arise and cease. If one can apply effort in this way, then our boundless karmic obstacles can, in a single moment, become pure and still as empty space. And if one can do this, then the power to grant or take away good and ill fortune and length or shortness of life lies in our own hands, and heaven and earth and the ghosts and spirits can do nothing about it — how much less can the spirits who oversee transgressions take away our tally!

In Yizhou of the Ming dynasty — that is, present-day Taiyuan in Shanxi — there was a man named Wang Yongyu, a man of generous and steady character. In ordinary life he served the Emperor Lord Wenchang with great care and reverence, and with several good friends he formed a society in his village. Every New Year’s Day they took turns to build an altar and pray for blessings at the traveling shrine of the Emperor Lord Wenchang on the summit of Mount Yunzhong. In the society there was a man named Yu Lin, known for his filial devotion and scrupulous conduct; people came from far and near to study under him and acknowledge him as their teacher. There was also a man named Yu Congzhou, of extraordinary appearance and commanding bearing, of talent eight measures deep, and with a first-rate gift for speech and writing. Everyone greatly admired and deferred to these two talented men.

On New Year’s Day of the xinyou year of the Zhengtong reign, Wang Yongyu went early to the shrine of Emperor Wenchang and lodged inside it. At night he had a dream in which he saw the Emperor Lord Wenchang ascending the hall, while all the City Gods of the realm gathered in the hall to report to the Lord the list of those to be admitted in the provincial examination. A spirit wearing a court cap and a red robe, holding a great register in his hands, presented it before the Lord and asked him to sign and approve it. Wang Yongyu secretly asked the spirit holding the register: ‘On the list of those admitted in Shanxi province, are there the names of Wang Yongyu, Yu Lin, and Yu Congzhou?’ The register-bearing spirit said: ‘No.’ After a while, when the City Gods had all withdrawn and were waiting to one side, the spirit in the red robe carried the register up to the hall, knelt, and presented it to the Lord for inspection. The Lord reviewed it one by one, and under the name of each admitted candidate drew a mark of approval. Sometimes the Lord hesitated a long while without marking. The red-robed spirit then announced the Lord’s instruction: ‘It is still to be entrusted to the City Gods of each province to speedily ascertain the generous sons of families that have accumulated hidden virtue, and to report their names, so as to replace the places in the register that the Lord has not approved.’ At this point Wang Yongyu was hiding beneath a pillar beside the hall, when suddenly he heard a call from within the hall summoning Wang Yongyu to enter the hall and have audience with the Lord. Wang Yongyu crawled on the ground below the hall steps, and was summoned to the Lord’s seat to present himself. The Lord said: ‘Matters of official rank and examination success are the secret records of the heavenly court, and may not be lightly divulged. Because for more than ten years you have been as constant as a single day, serving me with the utmost sincerity and earnestness, I have summoned you here to explain it to you. Your grandfather was utterly simple and scrupulous, supporting himself by his own labor, and never once did he mistreat anyone; long ago you were already recorded for the upper list of the provincial examination, so as to make manifest the retribution for your grandfather’s loyal and generous transmission of the family tradition. But because throughout your life, whenever you met gods or Buddhas, you bowed your head, yet always silently prayed only for your own examination success to go as you wished, and for your wife, née Yang, to recover from her illness, and for husband and wife to grow old together; while your aged mother was still living at home, and you never once prayed for the gods and Buddhas to protect her — for this reason your examination rank has been lowered by two grades, and so you will be admitted at the fifty-third place on the lower list. You should change this selfish attitude and behavior, and no longer offend the heart of Heaven!’ Having heard the Lord’s explanation, Wang Yongyu kept kowtowing and begging pardon. The Lord spoke again: ‘Zhou Ji, who is in the same society as you, is the first-place graduate of this year’s provincial examination in this province.’ At that time, among the members of the society, Zhou Ji was the most timid and weak, and his learning and writing were inferior to the others; hearing this, Wang Yongyu was quite astonished and taken aback; and so he bowed his head and asked the Lord the reason Zhou Ji would pass as first in the province this year. The Lord said: ‘Zhou Ji’s father and grandfather were both scholars, and never did a single word of theirs enter a government office in litigation, nor did they ever commit licentiousness. For three generations, the Zhou family, grandfather, father, and son, never once spoke of another’s shortcoming nor exposed a single evil deed of another. Moreover, Zhou Ji’s great-grandfather once wrote an essay called A Treatise on a Hundred Forbearances to exhort the people of the world, and by it transformed no small number of people. Therefore the fathers and sons, grandfathers and grandsons of the Zhou family have, in simplicity, plainness, and silence, been cultivating blessed retribution for more than sixty years. This is the highest kind of hidden virtue, and others do not know of it. The Most High God has therefore especially commended it, and has already recorded that the Zhou family shall flourish for three generations. That Zhou Ji now takes first place in the provincial examination is only the beginning of the Zhou family’s blessings!’ Wang Yongyu bowed again and asked the Lord: ‘Yu Lin and Yu Congzhou, who are in the same society as I, I wonder whether the two of them have passed?’ The Lord then inspected the register of the scholars of Taiyuan, and with an unhappy look on his face said: ‘Yu Lin should originally have been able to pass one examination, but because in serving his parents he committed the fault of inward faultfinding, and moreover was always harsh in criticizing others, contrary to all reason, and further arrogantly proclaimed himself a gentleman, therefore his examination rank has been taken away, and he will be destitute and frustrated all his life!’ Wang Yongyu asked the Lord again: ‘What is meant by inward faultfinding in serving one’s parents?’ The Lord said: ‘Toward his parents, Yu Lin, in words and conduct, put on the appearance of obedience and filial devotion; but in his heart he did not approve, and merely forced himself to show no sign of it. Outwardly he seemed to comply with his parents in everything, while his true nature daily drew further away. This kind of filial piety, self-deceiving and deceptive, is simply to regard one’s parents as strangers! You should know that to deceive the world and steal a name by false and hypocritical words and deeds angers the spirits most of all; that is why he was punished. As for Yu Congzhou, he was by nature a heaven-endowed talent. At twenty-six he should have passed the presented-scholar examination, in his early thirties he should have reached the office of censor, at forty-five he should have been promoted to Grand Master of Works, concurrently holding the offices of Director of Agriculture and Minister of Justice; at fifty-four he should have retired from the post of Junior Guardian, lived to sixty-nine, and obtained a peaceful end. But because from the age of seventeen, when he entered school, he relied on his talent and scorned others, in his speech constantly satirizing and ridiculing, and mocking and teasing others with double meanings, the underworld has recorded his frivolous verbal offenses, which have already reached more than two thousand four hundred and seventy. The Most High God was therefore enraged, and has already recorded him in the black register of hidden evil, and has taken away all the examination success allotted in his destiny. If he still does not repent, then when his offenses reach three thousand, his lifespan will be taken away. And his sons and grandsons will further be punished by falling into beggary! For these frivolous verbal offenses wound the harmonious qi between heaven and earth, and offend the taboos of the spirits; therefore the sin of this verbal karma is equal to the sins of killing living beings and of licentiousness — you must be especially careful and cautious!’ After a long while, the Lord gave further instruction: ‘Of the evil karma of licentiousness, killing, and verbal offense, even a hair’s breadth committed will have its retribution; there is no need to speak further of that. But as for the two evil karmas of licentiousness and killing, those who love themselves will know to abstain and not commit them; whereas as for mockery with the lips and casual ridicule and sarcasm — this heart that hides a knife in a smile and secretly harms others, once it becomes a habit, is very hard for one to become aware of. In the end even one’s speech, countenance, and heart all become frivolous. And these verbal evils are all recorded by the ghosts and spirits, so that baleful calamities follow after. A destiny that should have enjoyed the greatest blessings is in a moment turned into a destiny of poverty and lowliness — it is truly too pitiful, and too frightening! You should widely exhort the people of the world to take this as a warning, and no longer trouble me, when signing the register, with so much labor and hesitation!’ Wang Yongyu bowed twice more to the Lord and withdrew. At that moment the great bell of Emperor Wenchang’s shrine had already sounded, and Wang Yongyu woke with a start; outside, the cock had already crowed three times. Wang Yongyu therefore went to the shrine, bowed in gratitude to the Emperor Lord Wenchang, and taking up his brush wrote down this dream. When the results were posted in autumn, Zhou Ji had indeed taken first place in Shanxi province. Wang Yongyu thereupon made the record of this dream public, to warn the people of the world.

Chan Master Guangxiao An of the Song dynasty, while in samādhi, saw two monks talking. At first heavenly beings stood beside them in protection and even listened to their conversation; in time the heavenly beings dispersed. Not long after, evil ghosts appeared beside them, spitting and cursing them, and even sweeping with brooms the footprints the two monks had left. This was because the two monks had begun by discussing the Buddhadharma, then gone on to idle talk of household matters, and finally to talk of fame, gain, and profit. You should know that when renunciates talk of worldly matters they are already detested and blamed by ghosts and spirits; how much more so today, when the deeds of the people of the world in body, speech, and mind go far beyond this! Then how will they be blamed by ghosts and spirits? The very thought of it is to be feared!

A man’s lifespan, having already been reduced because of the offenses he has committed, is further punished by poverty and hardship in life and the breaking up of his family; and he constantly meets with sorrow and disaster!

From this sentence down to ‘when his tally is exhausted, he dies,’ all of it speaks of the matter of diminishing the tally of life. Because the deceitful and concealing conduct of the ungood is perceived by the spirits, so that their tally of life is reduced; and therefore poverty, the breaking up of the family, and sorrow follow one upon another. That goodness is blessed and licentiousness is visited with calamity is the necessary principle of creation. If a man wishes to draw near to the auspicious and avoid the inauspicious, he must certainly reform his faults and turn toward good; and the key to this lies in first governing the mind. He should examine the deeds of his own body, speech, and mind, and may not be self-indulgent and careless so as to fall into the net of evil karma. Moreover, one should admonish oneself in every part: for example, mind and mouth should instruct each other. The mind tells the mouth: ‘Mouth, O mouth! You should speak of good things and say good words; above all, do not say what ought not to be said!’ And the mind tells the body: ‘Body, O body! You should practice with diligence; do not be lazy and slothful!’ Even for a single day or hour, a single moment or thought, even for a single instant, one should be thus simple and silent, restraining one’s own mind, guarding one’s own mouth, governing one’s own body. If one continues so without interruption for long, one will naturally no longer be moved in mind by the influence of outer conditions; and at that point the mind reaches a state of pure stillness free of desire, and the whole of it is good! How then could one be stripped of his tally of life by the spirits, and reduced to poverty, a broken family, and sorrow?
A Story:

Qian Ruoyu, magistrate of Fengfu county, was a sinister and crafty man. In his youth he had already been appointed to office, and mostly he could not finish his term but was removed for some reason. In his later years his life grew even more straitened: his sons and daughters died one after another, and he himself sank to the point where he could not keep himself in food and clothing. So he prayed to the gods; and he dreamed that a spirit told him: ‘Qian Ruoyu, because you have committed too much evil karma, your lifespan, after the deductions, has already been entirely taken away by the spirits. Yet you still come to me complaining of the misery of poverty and the destruction of your family — you are foolish beyond words!’
All men detest the man who does evil!

The Jade Pivot Scripture says: ‘If a man does not cultivate good karma, Heaven will surely behead his spirit and seize his bodily soul, so that his spirit and soul are thrown into confusion, and he is detested and rejected by others!’ Those who today hate others for mistreating them — how would they know that this is Heaven beheading and seizing their spirit and soul, so that they meet with rebuffs everywhere and are detested by people? If one is fortunate enough to know this fact today, one should wash one’s heart and change one’s face, reform evil and turn toward good. For the heart of Heaven is kind and forgiving, and it does not punish those who repent and mend their ways; therefore the offenses committed in the past can be redeemed, and from now on, reforming and turning to good, one’s future is still one of brightness. So whether one knows by birth or knows through hardship, so long as one reforms and turns to good, the success is the same. I hope above all that no one will abandon himself in despair!

And why is the man who does evil detested by all? Because fairness naturally dwells in the human heart, and because the conscience is originally good — the innate moral knowledge is something everyone possesses from the start! But I hope everyone will extend this one thought: when one sees good, to fear only that one may fall behind others; when one sees what is not good, to dread it as though reaching one’s hand into scalding water. Thus one may spur oneself on and cultivate to the state in which there is good and no evil. If one merely detests others’ evil in vain while failing to remove one’s own evil, how can one escape being detested by others?

Lai Junchen of the Tang dynasty, when he served as censor, took bribes and perverted the law, and the number of innocent people he wronged to death was beyond counting. In the end he was condemned by the court on a charge of treason and publicly executed in the marketplace. After Lai Junchen was beheaded, many who hated him rushed forward in a swarm, fighting to be first to eat his flesh, gouge out his eyes, and seize his heart; in less than a moment his corpse had been eaten clean by the crowd!

In the Song dynasty the ministers Ding Wei and Lord Kou Lai were both officials at court. At that time, when the common people of the realm spoke of Lord Kou Lai, they would certainly call him a loyal minister; when they spoke of Ding Wei, they would certainly call him a treacherous minister. When they heard of a good deed, they would certainly attribute it to Lord Kou Lai — though in fact it was not necessarily he who did it! And when they heard of an evil deed, they would certainly lay the blame on Ding Wei — though in fact it was not necessarily he who did it either!

The Song dynasty prime minister Qin Hui deceived his sovereign and ruined the state, and destroyed loyal and good men. For a thousand years, none in the world has failed to detest Qin Hui’s treachery; while for Yue Fei’s utter loyalty in serving his country, none in later ages has failed to revere his example. In front of the Yue Wang Shrine by West Lake in Hangzhou there stand iron statues of Qin Hui and his wife, née Wang, kneeling before Yue Wang’s tomb, and beside them hangs a wooden hand. No matter how far or near, whoever comes to pay respects at Yue Wang’s tomb admires his utter loyalty in serving his country; and after bowing to Yue Wang, they all take up the wooden hand and beat the iron images of Qin Hui and his wife.

Taking these three examples together, the common people have no mind of private liking or private disliking; yet the reason they share the same likes and the same dislikes is that this is the human heart’s response to good and evil!
Punishment and calamity follow after him.

The Perfected One of the Great Void said: ‘If another shifts his calamity onto me, then I will repay him with blessing and virtue. If one can do this, then the qi of blessing and virtue will always issue from me, while the qi of harm and heavy calamity will naturally arise from the evil man.’ Here it says that punishment and calamity follow close upon the evil man: it is because the qi of harm and heavy calamity constantly abides on the evil man, and so punishment and calamity are bound to him.

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘The living beings of the Jambudvipa world of the south dwell within the evil world of the five turbidities! The living beings of this world will not cultivate the ten good karmas, but devote themselves wholly to making evil karma: killing, stealing, licentiousness, lying, frivolous speech, harsh speech, double-tongued speech, greed, anger, wrong views, failure to be filial to parents, failure to revere the Three Jewels — and further, they rage and contend with one another, slander and insult one another, give free rein to their thoughts, and make unlawful demands. From such causes and conditions they summon retribution in the form of weapons, famine, disease, death, natural disasters, and man-made calamities.’ From this it may be seen that it is always a matter of doing it oneself and receiving it oneself, of eating the fruit of one’s own evil — all summoned by oneself, and not made by anyone else! Yet the drawing near to the auspicious and the avoidance of the inauspicious is decided in the single thought of the present mind, and heaven and hell will appear before one’s eyes. If there truly were someone who cultivated the ten good karmas and yet received evil retribution, such a principle absolutely does not exist!

In the Han dynasty, Liang Tong petitioned the court to increase the severity of the laws and penalties, but the court did not accept his proposal. Later Liang Tong had a dream in which a spirit told him: ‘Liang Tong! Though the court was fortunate enough not to follow your advice, the underworld has already recorded your offense. Today you wished to use punishments to poison the people of the world — your intent was indeed most cruel and venomous. How then can your sons and grandsons escape the calamity of punishment? By this conduct you have offended Heaven; even if you pray, it is of no use!’ Afterward Liang Tong’s sons all died by violence; and by the time of Liang Ji, the evil was piled even deeper, and in the end the emperor issued an edict exterminating the clan, and the whole household was beheaded.
Auspiciousness and blessings all keep far away from him.

You should know that ‘the Way of Heaven has no favorites; it favors only the good man.’ If a man can forsake evil and do good, be reverent and careful with himself, and accord with the principle of Heaven, then naturally in stillness his mind will be joined with the Way of Heaven, and in movement his conduct will meet with auspiciousness and blessing. If a man’s mind and conduct are contrary to this, then what we can see is that he cannot escape the punishments of the world, and what we cannot see is that he is punished by the ghosts and spirits. Therefore the evil man has his tally of life reduced by the ghosts and spirits and dies young; and auspiciousness and blessing all keep far away from him, while unexpected calamity and punishment follow after him — this cannot be avoided.

Once there was a scholar named Wang Sheng, whose heart was sinister and crafty, and whose deeds also went against the principle of Heaven. On one occasion he sat for the autumn examination, and his essay was very well written; the presiding examiner, his own examining officer, wished to place him at the head of the list. But when the time came to fill in the roster, Wang Sheng’s examination paper suddenly could not be found; only after the roster was complete did Wang Sheng’s paper fall out from the examining officer’s sleeve. The examining officer was exceedingly regretful, and secretly met with Wang Sheng, promising that when an opportunity arose he would compensate him with another vacancy. Not long after this, the examining officer was transferred to a post in the bureau of appointments. Wang Sheng, meanwhile, had purchased his way into the Imperial College by contributing grain. When Wang Sheng sat the examination again, it happened that the examining officer was serving in the bureau of examination and selection. Seeing Wang Sheng, he was overjoyed, and secretly instructed that a fine vacancy be reserved for Wang Sheng through the opportunity of a special grace selection. But when the time of the grace selection arrived, the examining officer had to leave his post temporarily and return home to observe mourning for his father. Three years passed; when his mourning was complete and the court again employed him, he was once more appointed to a post in the selection bureau. By this time Wang Sheng, because of his seniority, ought to be selected and appointed to office, and a salary of ten thousand taels of gold was to be had within days! But within a few days Wang Sheng had to take mourning leave at home because of his mother’s death. After so many twists and turns, the examining officer, pitying Wang Sheng for his truly poverty-stricken fate, recommended him to the provincial governor as a family tutor, whereby in three years he could also receive a thousand taels of gold in salary. Yet before a month had passed, the provincial governor unexpectedly lost his office over an old matter. Throughout Wang Sheng’s life he repeatedly met with wonderful opportunities, yet all of them came to nothing. Wang Sheng felt exceedingly wronged in his heart, and so fell gravely ill and lay on a sickbed for three years. One day Wang Sheng suddenly awakened and said: ‘All of this is the evil fruit produced by my habit of accumulating evil in ordinary times!’ Afterward Wang Sheng’s illness gradually healed through repentance and reform, and so Wang Sheng did good for the rest of his life.

Mr. Xue Xiyuan once said: ‘As for the blessings and emoluments of this world, if one does not keep a heart of anxious diligence and vigilant effort, blessings and emoluments cannot be gathered to one; and if one does not do deeds that aid men and benefit beings, blessings and emoluments cannot be matched to one.’ These words are truly reasonable!
Baleful spirits and evil stars likewise send down disaster upon the man who does evil.

The evil stars are the deities in Heaven who govern all the disasters and calamities of the human world. You should know that a man living in this world, every day and indeed every seasonal period, is presided over by the radiance of the stars. Because the man who does evil constantly has a darkened mind, the black qi of his body rises upward, and he naturally summons evil by evil; therefore baleful spirits and evil stars descend upon his head, and disaster follows after. If a man does good, then because his mind-ground is bright, the aura of evil gradually disperses, and baleful spirits and evil stars cannot flee from him fast enough — how could they send disaster down upon him? Alas! It is truly because a man makes his own misdeeds that baleful spirits and evil stars send disaster upon him. In truth, the disaster is not sent by the baleful spirits and evil stars; it is summoned by himself! It is not that the baleful spirits and evil stars are bad; it is that he himself is bad! Having learned this fact, how can a man fail to stand in awe, correct and examine his own faults, and so win back the heart of Heaven?

In the district of Jucheng in Shandong province there was a man named Ma Changshi, who, relying on his cleverness and ability, ran wild everywhere and committed every kind of evil. One day a small comet fell from the sky and landed in his courtyard, turning into a great stone. From that time on, Ma Changshi’s household knew no end of lawsuits, was afflicted with illness, and was plagued by quarrels and slander one after another. After a little more than a year, Ma Changshi died and his family scattered. The Ma family house stood empty with no one living in it. And around this great stone, for several feet in every direction, there appeared a faint purple color, and patterns like written characters showed upon it — it is still there today!
When the evil man’s tally of life has been wholly reduced, the evil man dies!

This sentence is the Most High’s earnest and heartfelt admonition handed down to the people of the world. The habitual tendency of living beings to do evil is truly hard to uproot, and they do nothing but unwholesome and evil karma! And their own vast karmic consciousness is like fat feeding a fire, each consuming the other; the days of their life pass one by one until their tally of life has been wholly taken away — that is, the time of death has come. And even then their guilt is more than death can atone for! They must further suffer retribution according to the evil karma made during their lives! Thereupon their consciousness falls into the three evil paths of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell, and suffers there, and the pain they then receive is endless! Who says that death is the end of everything, that then there is nothing? On the contrary, after death it is worse than ever, without end! Speaking of this, one cannot help but cry out aloud and weep. You should know that ‘the human body is easily lost, and fixed karma is hard to escape’; one can only hope that men of benevolence and aspiration will believe this principle without a doubt! While a single breath remains, one can still repent and wipe away sky-filling sins; but if one drifts on in careless idleness day after day, then a hundred years of time will pass swift as an arrow; and when at the end of life the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind separate, remorse and regret will come too late!

Once there was an old man who after death met King Yama, and blamed him for not having written to inform him in advance. King Yama said: ‘Your eyes grew dim — that was my first letter to you! Your ears grew deaf — that was my second letter to you! Your teeth decayed — that was my third letter to you! Your body grows weaker day by day — I do not know how many letters I have already written to inform you; how can you still say I never wrote to inform you?’ And there was a young man who after death met King Yama and likewise blamed him, saying: ‘My eyes were bright, my ears keen, my teeth sharp, and my body very strong — King Yama, why did you summon me without first writing to inform me?’ King Yama replied: ‘I did write to inform you too! Did you not see that your neighbor to the east died at thirty or forty, and your neighbor to the west died at ten or twenty? And there are even infants of a full year, and children, who die; all of these were my letters to you!’ Therefore human life is impermanent, like the morning dew: once a single breath does not come back, this body becomes a mere husk! In the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters it is told that the Buddha asked his disciples: ‘How long is a human life?’ One disciple answered: ‘A human life lasts but a few days.’ The Buddha said: ‘You do not yet know the Way.’ The Buddha asked another disciple, who answered: ‘It lasts but the time of a meal.’ The Buddha said: ‘You do not know the Way either.’ The Buddha asked yet another disciple, and this disciple answered: ‘A human life lasts but the space of a single breath!’ The Buddha said: ‘Excellent! Excellent! You know the Way!’

Chan Master Tianru of the Lion Grove in Suzhou during the Yuan dynasty once said: ‘The Buddhas and patriarchs appear in this world for the sole sake of the one great matter of birth and death beneath our own feet — that is, the great matter of which it is said, “We do not know whence we come at birth, nor whither we go at death.” If one is born thus and dies thus, the whole great earth is shrouded by it! And from ancient times until now, there is not one person who has not been swallowed up by the great sea of birth and death. Let us not speak of ancient times; consider only your own life: think back ten or twenty years — how many of your relatives and friends have already died? Let us not speak first of others; speak of yourself. This present body of the four elements, earth, water, fire, and wind, is borrowed and falsely taken as “I”; from morning to night you cherish it in a thousand ways and nourish it with a thousand things; yet it changes and passes on without a moment’s pause, gradually wasting away! Unknowingly, the day of the thirtieth of the twelfth month — the day of death — arrives; at that time you feel your hands and feet in confusion, in agony like a crab dropped into boiling water! Where have all your heroic feelings and lofty ambitions gone? And after death the color of the body begins to change, foul and filthy, until it is past enduring; though there be close kin of your own flesh and blood, at that time they will not be willing to look at you straight on! Where then is all the love and affection of your life? For this reason the patriarchs said: if a man’s single breath does not return, he is no different from dust and soil! The road ahead is a vast blank; he does not know where to go. To die and be burned just like this is truly pitiable! How much more so, after death, must one receive retribution according to the karma one has made — this is the matter that counts! What then does it mean to receive retribution according to karma? It means that everything you have done in your life is karma! Where there is karma, there will be its fruit! You should know that the fruit of retribution follows the power of karma as the shadow follows the form. This body has already died, yet this consciousness-spirit falls into hell, or into the realm of hungry ghosts, or into the realm of animals, turning about in rebirth, and thereby receives immeasurable, boundless suffering! That is the realm of retribution; this is the root of birth and death. And what is called the root of karma is precisely the single thought of your present mind! From beginningless time, because of greed, anger, and delusion, because of ignorance, affliction, deluded thoughts, and the mad mind, when it comes into contact with outer objects and meets outer conditions, it follows the dust of sound and chases the dust of form, so that you are utterly turned upside down and there is no karma you do not make — this is the root of your birth and death and rebirth! Therefore when one thinks of the great matter of birth and death, even an iron man will feel disheartened! For this reason the Buddhas and patriarchs, moving great compassion and giving rise to deep pity, teach you to study the Buddha’s teaching and practice, to investigate Chan and study the Way, to have you sweep away deluded thoughts and the mad mind, to recognize your own master, to know your original face before your parents were born. Therefore take advantage of the time when your eyes are still bright and your legs still strong: quickly become a pure and liberated person! Then when the end of life comes, you will obtain great benefit — that is, what is called freedom in birth and death, without the least obstruction, coming and going freely! This is called escaping birth and death, and such a person is truly a great man!’

This says that in a man’s whole body, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there are star-spirits watching and examining.
