The star-spirits of the Three Terraces and the Lord of the Northern Dipper constantly hover above a man’s head, recording the sins each man commits, and according to the lightness or gravity of his offenses they take away from his lifespan.

In a man’s lifespan, twelve years make one ji, and a hundred days are called one suan. The star-spirits of the Three Terraces govern a man’s long life or early death; the Lord of the Northern Dipper governs a man’s good and evil. The Sutra of the Causes and Conditions of Karmic Retribution also says: ‘The qi of the seven stars constantly gathers into a single star, located above a man’s head at a distance of three inches from the crown. If he is a man who does good, then the light that appears above his head is bright; if he is a man who does evil, then the light that appears above his head is dark. If he is a man of great good, the light above his head appears even brighter; if he is a man of great evil, the light above his head is extinguished and gone. This light is something ordinary people cannot see, but ghosts and spirits see it perfectly clearly!’

Lou Shide, a great minister of the Tang dynasty, enjoyed the favor and trust of Emperor Gaozong and made great contributions to the court. One morning when Lou Shide rose from bed, he suddenly saw a star-official who told him: ‘You once killed two people by mistake; for this offense twelve years must be taken from your lifespan, and the starlight above your head is about to be extinguished!’ That very day Lou Shide felt his consciousness somewhat dim and confused, and so he told those around him: ‘All my life I have been careful in my conduct; only because I killed two people by mistake am I now to die twelve years early!’ Before long, Lou Shide passed away.

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said: ‘Throughout his life, Mr. Lou Shide was known for his brilliance and generosity, and he was an important minister of the Tang dynasty; yet even he could not avoid committing a fault and having twelve years taken from his lifespan. How much more so for ordinary people, who do not know how much evil karma they have made! Seeing Mr. Lou’s example, can one fail to be careful?’

There are also the three corpse-spirits, which dwell inside a man’s body. Whatever a man thinks in mind, speaks with mouth, intends in thought, or utters in words can never be hidden from the three corpse-spirits. On every gengshen day — the day on which the heavenly gods decide men’s good and evil — the three corpse-spirits ascend to the tribunal of the Heavenly Emperor and truthfully report the man’s offenses.

This says that in a man’s single mind, at the faintest stirring of a thought, there are spirits watching and examining. The upper corpse-spirit, the Green Maiden, named Peng Ju, dwells in a man’s head; she makes a man think much and desire much, so that his eyes grow dim and his hair falls out. The middle corpse-spirit, the White Maiden, named Peng Zhi, dwells in a man’s intestines; she makes a man fond of eating and drinking and forgetful of matters, and fond of doing evil. The lower corpse-spirit, the Blood Maiden, named Peng Qiao, dwells in a man’s feet; she makes a man lustful and fond of killing, so that his hands and feet, his four limbs, and his five viscera and six bowels are disturbed and uneasy. All that the three corpse-spirits do is aimed at making a man die sooner, so that they may go out and become ghosts themselves, enjoying the offerings of blood sacrifice. Therefore on the day of gengshen, taking advantage of a man’s sound sleep, they go up with the seven bodily souls within his body to the tribunal of the Heavenly Emperor and recount the man’s offenses. So it is said that of all the sounds a man makes with mind, mouth, intention, and speech, the three corpse-spirits hear them most clearly among the ghosts and spirits. People today do not know to examine themselves, restrain themselves, purify their minds, and lessen their desires; instead they vainly rely on the Daoist practice of guarding the gengshen day and removing the shen day, thinking that by this they can cut off the road by which the three corpse-spirits go up to the heavenly tribunal to lodge their complaints. Such a practice is merely deceiving oneself in vain. You should know that so long as one’s own mind-ground is bright and upright, ghosts and spirits will naturally withdraw — what is there in the three corpse-spirits to worry about? The Song dynasty Mr. Cheng also wrote a poem on the night watches, saying: ‘Gengshen I do not guard, nor do I doubt; this mind forever with the Way abides. Heaven on high has known my deeds throughout — let the three Pengs say what they will besides.’
On the last day of every lunar month, the Stove God does the same!

This speaks of a man’s whole household: in every movement and in every place of dwelling, there are ghosts and spirits watching and examining. The Stove God governs the lives of a whole family, and so is called the Master of Destinies. All the offenses, great and small, committed by the men and women, old and young of a household, the Stove God perceives without the slightest omission; and at the end of each month he reports directly to the Two Luminaries of yin and yang — that is, the deities of the sun and moon — and records the offenses in a black register. In the conduct of people in the world, they know only how to crave the pleasure of the moment — how could they ask whether there is a Stove God in the house recording the offenses they commit?

In the district of Zhun there was a scholar who once, after drinking too much wine, molested a maidservant in his household. The maidservant, however, had a keen sense of shame and firmly refused her master’s advances, and so was able to seize the chance to escape his importuning. At that time it was the very last day of the lunar month. When the scholar was sleeping, at the fourth watch, his wife suddenly woke him, saying: ‘Just now I saw a star-spirit wearing a square cap and a black robe, riding a swift horse in flight; he carried registers with him, and he pointed at me with his hand and then galloped away. I could not hear clearly, nor do I know what he said to me; I only felt his divine majesty, and before I knew it I woke in fright.’ Hearing his wife say this, the scholar felt his hair stand on end all over, but he only answered: ‘The spirit in your dream must have been the Stove God!’ Afterward the scholar married the maidservant off to another, and then explained to his wife: ‘Your dream of the Stove God pointing something out to you was because I had once molested this maidservant; she escaped it by her firm resistance. I never expected that on that very night the Stove God would give warning. I think that although the matter was not carried out, the evil thought was already in my mind, and so it was recorded by the Stove God and reported to the heavenly bureaus. Before this I did not dare explain it to you, for fear you would doubt, and for fear you would make things hard for this maidservant. Today I explain it to you, first to commend this maidservant’s chastity, and second to expose the fault I committed and make confession to you.’
[Appendix]

Luo Zhen, a man of Jiangxi in the Ming dynasty, wrote a book called How Master Yu Jingyi Met the Stove God. Elder Master Jingkong once gave an exposition of it; its content is most wonderful and detailed, and deeply absorbing, so it is omitted here.

Whenever a man commits an offense, he cannot escape the scrutiny of the spirits: for a grave offense he has twelve years taken from his lifespan, and for a light fault a hundred days are deducted — this is absolutely certain and without error.

This sentence summarizes the meaning of the foregoing. It explains that in a man’s whole life and body, his one mind and one household, there are spirits watching and examining everywhere, and the purpose is to teach men to be cautious when alone. Whenever a man is conceived and born, the length of his lifespan, and its increase or decrease, are all recorded in Heaven. The Most High commanded the various spirits: ‘You are to examine the good and evil of the human world, speaking once every three days, memorializing once every ten days, and settling accounts once every hundred days. If a man cultivates good and establishes merit, he may have his lifespan extended; if by any chance he commits an offense, his lifespan is at once reduced by a suan or a ji.’ Therefore offenses are great and small, and the taking of a ji or a suan has its vast differences!

Master Wang Biru of Tiantai in the Ming dynasty, in his youth, passed the provincial examination in the bingwu year of the Wanli reign and was appointed by the Ministry of Personnel as magistrate of Xingan county. From childhood he had observed the four precepts against killing, stealing, licentiousness, and lying; but afterward, because he became an official, he abandoned the observance of the precepts. In the wuwu year he went to the capital to have audience with the emperor. On the way, when his boat was moored at Wuhu, his soul was led by ghost-soldiers down to the underworld. He saw a king of the underworld seated in the great hall, with two judges seated to the king’s left and right. The king called his name and rebuked him, saying: ‘Wang Biru, your lifespan should have ended in the eighth month of the bingchen year; that you have been able to live until today is entirely due to the power of the merit of your fasting and precepts. Why did you abandon the precepts?’ Having said this, the king ordered an attendant to bring the register for Wang Biru to see. Wang Biru saw that beneath his name the years and months were all recorded, but after the eighth month of the bingchen year the record was blank. Having read it, he kowtowed to the king and said: ‘In official life it was somewhat inconvenient for me to keep the fast and precepts, and so I abandoned them; truly it was unavoidable!’ The king said: ‘What you say has some reason, but what is to be done, since your allotted lifespan in the world of the living is already exhausted?’ Having said this, he ordered him driven into hell; and at once many fearsome-looking evil ghosts came forward, showing every sign of wanting to bind and seize him. At this point the judge seated to the king’s left asked the king’s instruction, saying: ‘It would do no harm to fetch and examine Wang Biru’s deeds after he broke the precepts.’ Before long the jailers carried in two great chests of documents, all of them the case files from the time Wang Biru served as magistrate of Xingan county. Every letter he had written, every official document, and every scrap of paper he had casually written on in ordinary days was there; and from each of them qi rose up, in green, black, red, and white, all different. The king ordered the jailers to sort them into categories, gathering like with like: first the black and the green were picked out and placed together, then the white ones were gathered, and then the red ones gathered together. At this point those gathered as green vanished, the black ones shrank to the size of a chopstick, while the red ones alone blazed out conspicuously. Wang Biru, watching from the side, saw that the pile of clearly red documents consisted of the Diamond Sutra and the Essay on Cherishing Life that he had had printed. When the jailers had finished sorting, the king’s voice and tone softened somewhat, and he said to the judge on his left: ‘Hm! He still knows how to accumulate virtue, and there is reason for him to live; then let his five sense organs be damaged but his body preserved, and let him live.’ So saying, he ordered the jailers to gouge out both his eyes and place them on a pillar of the great hall, where their gaze still shone bright in all four directions. At this point Wang Biru thought: ‘My eyes have been gouged out — how can I still see anything?’ In the instant of that thought, everything suddenly went dark, and the palace, the judges, and the jailers had all vanished. Afterward he felt someone pat him on the back, saying: ‘Wang Biru, go quickly! Go quickly!’ A moment later he stumbled and woke with a start; the next day both his eyes were blind, and so he abandoned his household and went to cultivate the Way. In time his practice opened into awakening, and his eyesight was restored. Thereupon Wang Biru traveled widely among the communities of Yunqi and Boshan, truly investigating and truly realizing, and also practicing the Great Compassion Repentance; and he lived another twelve years.

Having seen Wang Biru’s experience, you should know that apart from sages and worthies, no man goes a day without committing some fault; and what can win back the workings of fate is nothing but the ability to reform. Otherwise, since the earlier causes are already poor, and the evil karma made afterward keeps increasing, then though one may have many blessings and many sons, when the single breath does not return, none of it can be carried away; only the karma one has made follows oneself. At that time one sees only the toil of King Yama’s reckoning — can one’s family property be taken along? Can one’s sons and daughters take one’s place? Everyone should think this over carefully!

Fu Zhongxin of the Song dynasty was wealthy and fond of giving. But in the year he turned thirty-five he suddenly fell ill, and the illness turned critical. He even said himself that he had been to the underworld, where he met several old friends who asked him: ‘Benefactor! How did you come to be here?’ The old friends then bowed and inquired of an underworld official on his behalf. The official said: ‘Fu Zhongxin was destined for a life of hunger and cold; but because his heart loved to give and relieve others, he was able to build a fortune from nothing. His lifespan should have reached fifty-nine years, but because he did not burn incense and rose late in the morning, his blessings and lifespan have been cut away entirely as of today.’ The old friends said: ‘These two things are mere small faults — how could they be so serious?’ The official said: ‘Not burning incense shows a heart without reverence for heaven and earth; rising late shows thoughts of licentiousness — how can they be called small faults?’ Hearing this, everyone looked at Fu Zhongxin in some astonishment and said: ‘If a man of such generous virtue as Mr. Fu still has his lifespan cut short for these two things, then how can ordinary people carelessly indulge themselves?’ Before long, Fu Zhongxin died.

You should know that the most difficult thing to obtain in human life is a long lifespan, and it is also the lifespan that is taken away in the unseen realms. That is why the Most High taught these principles so earnestly and repeatedly: to warn the people of the world to watch carefully over the arising of their thoughts, and not to make the error of a single thought, so that they may enjoy long life, the first of the Five Blessings! The Most High is truly most compassionate toward the people of the world!
These offenses and evil karma, great and small, number several hundred; all who seek long life must first avoid these offenses and evil karma!

Here the Most High teaches men to begin by avoiding offenses. The several hundred matters spoken of here are all the offenses listed in this tract, from ‘acts without righteousness’ down to ‘death comes with it.’ The taking away of lifespan spoken of earlier teaches men to know fear and be on guard; now the speaking of long life teaches men to know what to aspire to, and to be brave in reforming faults and doing good. If one does not dare commit even a small fault, one will surely obtain the good retribution of long life.

In particular, those who study the Way all take the accumulation of good and the cultivation of their own virtue as their fundamental practice. In Confucianism this is called the four beginnings and the hundred practices; in Buddhism it is called the six paramitas and ten thousand practices; in Daoism it is the three thousand merits and eight hundred practices. All of these are ways of speaking of accumulating good and avoiding evil. Yet if one wishes to accumulate good and reform faults, nothing comes before comprehending the supreme wondrous Way; and if one wishes to comprehend the supreme wondrous Way, nothing is better than understanding one’s own original mind — for the mind is the substance of the Way, and the Way is the function of the mind. If a man can examine the mind and observe the nature, then the perfect and luminous substance will naturally appear before him, and the function of non-doing will naturally be accomplished; without borrowing any effort at all, he can leap straight beyond the farther shore. Had he not cultivated to the point where the mirror of the mind is clear and the divine pearl is utterly transparent, how could he cause all thoughts suddenly to depart, with not a hair’s breadth of defilement clinging to him, so that the source of the mind is at ease and he is decisively free from birth? Therefore the cultivator who understands the mind and embodies the Way is not entangled in his nature by the body, nor does he disorder his true mind by outer conditions; and in responding freely to things as they come, he naturally preserves within himself the principle of neither birth nor death — this is what is called the supreme, most true, wondrous Way! But those today who seek long life merely rely in vain on the methods of storing the essence and subduing the breath, of refining medicines and burning cinnabar, and then say that true immortality may be met with; they do not know that these are all outer paths, seeking the Dharma outside the mind!

There was a female immortal named Yang Zhengjian, whose cultivation would soon have brought her to ascend to the ranks of the Perfected. But the Most High God reproved her because when she was small, her parents were preparing money to pay their taxes, and Yang Zhengjian, seeing it, secretly picked out two particularly round and fine coins from the tax money and hid them — this is what is called concealing official property! Therefore the Most High God issued an order demoting Yang Zhengjian to remain in the human world for one more year. The Lady of Purple Emptiness and Lord Mao together, in the Palace of Pure Emptiness, were checking and verifying the gains and losses of the true immortals of the world; in one moment as many as forty-seven true immortals were struck off the list. After being struck off, they were reviewed once more, and only two were able to pass and be re-enrolled! This was because they had harbored thoughts of lust while cultivating the affairs of the supreme Perfected, and so they could not but have faults. The secret hiding of two coins was a very small fault, and yet the cultivation of an immortal, after weighing merits against faults, was still so severely condemned — how much more so for those who recklessly and carelessly fail to avoid committing faults!

In Liaofan’s Four Lessons for the Family by Mr. Yuan Liaofan of the Ming dynasty there is a detailed discussion of the methods of reforming faults, and a most penetrating one. Those who wish to understand further and emulate Liaofan should consult and study Elder Master Jingkong’s lectures on Liaofan’s Four Lessons, also titled The Way of Cultivating Blessings, Accumulating Virtue, and Creating Destiny; here it is omitted.

Whenever one is about to do something, one should first think whether it accords with principle. If it accords with principle, then advance and do it; if it does not accord with principle, then draw back and do not do it.

This section, down to ‘one should establish three hundred good deeds,’ sets out the Most High’s general outline of doing good and summoning blessing, first teaching men to practice every good, whereby they may summon blessed retribution. The Way is like a great road: to accord with the principle of Heaven and match the hearts of men, level and upright — this is the Way; to go against the principle of Heaven and offend the hearts of men, thorny and perilous — this is not the Way. In this tract, from ‘do not tread the crooked byways’ down to ‘give to others without regret,’ all of it is the Way, that is, doing good. From ‘acts without righteousness’ to ‘kills turtles and beats snakes,’ all of it is not the Way, that is, doing evil. And the two words ‘if it accords’ in ‘if it accords with the Way, advance; if it does not accord with the Way, withdraw’ are the most critical and demanding of effort; for right and wrong are distinguished only in the thought of the moment, while advance and retreat must be decided immediately. At this crucial juncture one must use the method of a clean cut, and must not have the least thought of hesitation! If the thought turns, one will fall again into the demon’s pass; therefore one must constantly examine oneself and be careful in every matter. For example: when family members go against one’s wishes, does one give rise to affliction? When living in comfort and plenty, does one give rise to lustful thoughts? When the household income is small, does one scheme to make money? When one’s fellow cultivators leave, does one grow dull and slothful? And so on through all such cases: all of them are enough to make one lose the mind of the Way and enter into what is contrary to principle. Therefore they may not be taken lightly!

And the ‘Way’ spoken of here is the ‘Way’ of which the Doctrine of the Mean says: ‘What Heaven confers is called the nature; to follow the nature is called the Way.’ In our daily life, whether speaking or keeping silent, whether moving or still, there is nowhere that is not the Way! One need only truly and deeply understand its principle, and one will practice it with great courage and diligence. The ancients said: ‘The great Way is not apart from what lies before you; yet what lies before you is hard to see. If you would know the true substance of the great Way, it is not apart from sound, form, speech, and words.’ The Daodejing says: ‘When the highest type of man hears the Way, he practices it diligently.’ The Scripture of Inner Observation says: ‘To know the Way is easy; to believe in the Way is hard. To believe in the Way is easy; to practice the Way is hard.’ The Avatamsaka Sutra says: ‘Faith is the source and mother of the Way and merit; it nurtures all roots of goodness. It cuts off the net of doubt and leads out of the river of craving; it reveals the supreme Way of nirvāṇa.’ For the substance of the Way is something every person already possesses in full; though one be drowned in ten thousand kinds of material desire, if one is willing to turn the light of a single thought back and shine it inward, then the true right and true wrong within cannot be hidden in the least! This is what is called ‘the substance in which the principle of Heaven never ceases.’ If one can expand it until it fills all, then though ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives pass, one will never fall again. Therefore if a man can unite knowing and doing, it is not difficult to transcend the ordinary and enter the sage! These are true words!

Once there was a farmer who had been bitten by a tiger. When someone spoke of tigers injuring people, everyone who heard was greatly alarmed; only this farmer’s face changed greatly, quite unlike the others. That a tiger injures people is something everyone knows; yet one who has not experienced it himself, on hearing of a tiger’s attack, is merely startled for a moment. But this farmer had himself suffered the pain of a tiger’s bite, and so his face changed greatly and his heart still quailed.

From this story we may know that when a man still does the things that go against the principle of Heaven, offend the hearts of men, and are thorny and perilous — the things called not the Way — it is because he has never truly known and experienced them. If he had truly known and experienced them, he would certainly never do the things that are not the Way.

Guan Ning, the great Confucian scholar of the Later Han dynasty, once hoed the ground and planted crops together with Hua Xin. On one occasion Guan Ning hoed up a piece of gold, and did not so much as glance at it; while Hua Xin picked up the gold and threw it aside. At that time the world was in disorder, and Guan Ning took refuge from the chaos in Liaodong. Gongsun Du of Liaodong treated Guan Ning with great courtesy; Guan Ning did not accept it and went to live on the mountain, and at that time many people followed him up the mountain. Once a neighbor’s ox trampled Guan Ning’s field; Guan Ning led the ox out to the wilderness to graze, and when the ox’s owner learned of it he felt exceedingly ashamed and apologized to Guan Ning. Gradually more and more people came to live where Guan Ning was; so Guan Ning began to lecture on learning, teaching the local people to understand propriety and righteousness and to know shame. If someone did not come to seek learning, Guan Ning would not meet with him. Guan Ning’s teaching soon spread throughout Liaodong, and the common people, influenced by his lofty morality, reformed their customs. Whenever Guan Ning met with Gongsun Du, he spoke only of matters pertaining to morality, and never once touched on the common affairs of the world. Gongsun Du considered Guan Ning most worthy, and so he stayed in Liaodong for thirty-seven years. Later, in obedience to an order from the court, he crossed the sea by boat to return to the capital. At that time a great wind suddenly arose at sea and the boat was about to capsize; the boatmen all cried out to Heaven and confessed their sins, begging Heaven to save their lives! Guan Ning then sat upright and said: ‘In all my life I, Guan Ning, have once gone without my cap in the morning, three times risen too late, and once gone to the privy without my cap; the faults I have committed in my whole life must be these alone!’ The other boats traveling with Guan Ning all sank, and only the boat Guan Ning sat in did not sink. When he reached the capital, the court wished to grant Guan Ning the office of Grand Master of the Palace; Guan Ning did not accept it. Hua Xin wished to yield his own post of Grand Commandant to Guan Ning, but Guan Ning also earnestly declined it to Hua Xin.

Guan Ning lived to the age of eighty-four before he died. In the wooden couch he sat on during his lifetime, the place that touched his knees had already worn through — for Guan Ning had not once sat with his legs sprawled out in fifty years!

When relatives or neighbors were poor and their households lacked rice, Guan Ning would certainly share his own rice to relieve them. When Guan Ning met one who was a son or daughter, he would certainly speak to him of the principle of filial devotion; when he met one who was a younger brother or disciple, he would certainly speak to him of the principle of fraternal respect; when he met one who was a subject or official, he would certainly speak to him of the principle of loyalty. Guan Ning’s countenance was not only reverent but his speech was gentle and compliant, and he could guide people toward good according to the matter at hand; therefore he was able to transform countless people!

All improper places — gambling dens, brothels, dance halls, opium houses, and the like — must be regarded as crooked byways, and one must resolutely draw back and not go to them. Even in a dark room, in a place where others can neither see nor hear, which is precisely the boundary where good and evil are first divided, one should be able to rectify the mind and make the will sincere, unwilling to deceive others in the slightest.

These two sentences single out from among the avoidance of faults the most essential ones, to admonish men; they are also the beginning of being a good person. ‘Do not tread the crooked byways’ means that from the very source of the mind one must set oneself squarely and uprightly: though a crooked path be but a hair’s breadth and the matter at stake ever so small, at this point one resolutely does not walk it — then one may know what one will do where the matter is great. ‘Do not deceive in the darkened chamber’ means that from the very source of the mind one must sweep oneself clean and bright: though one be in the most secret place in the house, where only oneself knows, one resolutely refuses to act carelessly — then one may know what one will do in the open. If one can be thus, then in accumulating merit and piling up virtue and doing all kinds of good deeds, one can carry it through with a single thread!

You should know that blessing is the reward for virtue; if there is the slightest mind of seeking blessing, that is a crooked byway! Therefore one should create blessings for one’s sons and grandsons, and should not seek blessings for them. To keep the family rules strictly, to honor simplicity and frugality, to teach farming and reading, and to accumulate hidden virtue widely — these are creating blessings for one’s sons and grandsons. But to enlarge fields and dwellings, to arrange marriages for advantage, to contend over a tenth of the profit, and to traffic in examination rank — these are seeking blessings for one’s sons and grandsons. You should know that creating blessings, though it looks plain and mild, can make a man’s descendants last long; while seeking blessings, though it looks bustling and lively, shortens the blessings of one’s descendants!

And name is the guest of reality — that is, name and reality must match. If there is the slightest mind of marketing oneself, that is, the mind of fishing for reputation and publicity, that is a crooked byway! Therefore one should cherish one’s name for this life, and should not market one’s name for this life. To study poetry and books diligently, to honor integrity, to be careful in what one takes and gives, and to pay attention to one’s dignified bearing — these are cherishing one’s name! But to vie in mutual advertisement, to strive to invite the favor of the powerful, to pursue the eccentric and provocative, and to cultivate cliquishness — these are marketing one’s name! Therefore those who cherish their name appear calm and auspicious, while those who market their name appear restless and clumsy!

In the Ming dynasty there was a man named Yang Zhu of Wuxian in Jiangsu, who rose to the office of Minister. One night he dreamed that he was strolling in a garden, and without thinking picked two plums from a tree and ate them. When he woke, he bitterly reproached himself, saying: ‘This is because I am ordinarily not clear enough in my understanding of righteousness and profit, that in my dream I should dream of stealing plums from another’s garden to eat!’ And Yang Zhu punished himself for this matter by eating nothing for several days.

Once there was an eight-year-old novice monk named Miaoyan who had already attained the spiritual powers of an arhat. Once he flew into a royal palace, and the queen wished to embrace him. Miaoyan said to the queen: ‘You must not embrace me; a queen should not come close to the body of a renunciate.’ The queen said: ‘You are no bigger than my youngest son; what harm is there in letting me embrace you?’ Miaoyan answered: ‘Let us take feeling as our comparison, as the queen has just said; but feeling always begins from what is small — just as a spark of fire can burn a plain a thousand miles wide, and as drops of water can wear through a stone as high as Mount Tai. Everything begins gradually, increasing little by little and growing from small to great; therefore the wise keep far from anything that arouses suspicion — this is what is called guarding against the smallest beginnings and stopping things before they spread!’

Yang Zhen of the Han dynasty was governor of Donglai. Once, passing through a county under his jurisdiction, the county magistrate, Wang Mi, was a man whom he had recommended. At night Wang Mi came with gold to visit Yang Zhen, and said: ‘In the darkness of night, no one will know of this.’ Yang Zhen said: ‘Heaven knows, earth knows, you know, and I know — how can you say no one will know?’ Hearing this, Wang Mi felt exceedingly ashamed. Afterward Yang Zhen’s office rose to the Three Excellencies.

He Cheng was a physician of brilliant medical skill. He had a patient surnamed Sun who had been ill for a long time without recovering; Sun had once summoned He Cheng to his home to treat him, and He Cheng had attended him several times. Sun’s wife then secretly said to He Cheng: ‘My husband has been ill for a long time, and the family’s goods are almost all pawned away; I am willing to repay the medical fees I owe with my body.’ Hearing this, He Cheng said to her sternly: ‘Why should Madam Sun speak such words? But please set your mind at ease and do not worry; I will certainly do my utmost to cure Mr. Sun. If I took this opportunity to violate you, it would not only make me a petty man forever, but would also cause you, madam, to lose your great chastity. And even if we could avoid the blame of others, you should know that the punishment of Heaven is hard to escape!’ Afterward He Cheng one night had a dream in which he came to a great government office, where a spirit said to him: ‘He Cheng, in practicing medicine you have saved lives and have merit; and moreover, when others were in hardship and danger, you did not violate their women. The Most High God therefore grants you an official post and fifty thousand strings of cash.’ Soon after He Cheng had this dream, the crown prince fell ill, and physicians of great skill were sought everywhere; in the end He Cheng was found. He Cheng prescribed but a single dose of medicine, and the prince’s illness was cured. Therefore the prince bestowed on He Cheng an official post and fifty thousand strings of cash — exactly as in his dream!

Accumulating virtue should be like accumulating money: pile it up gradually, and gradually it grows more. Piling up merit should be like building a wall: build gradually, and gradually it grows higher.

If virtue is not accumulated, it will not become lofty; if merit is not piled up, it will not become great. If one can be as earnest as a farmer hoping for the autumn harvest, and strive as hard as a merchant hoping to make a great profit; if today one accumulates a measure of virtue and tomorrow another, and today one piles up a measure of merit and tomorrow another, then even to cultivate to the state of an immortal is no difficult matter! To cultivate to be a celestial immortal one must perform one thousand three hundred good deeds; do one each day, and in only four years it can be accomplished. To cultivate to be an earthly immortal one must perform three hundred good deeds; do one each day, and in only one year it can be accomplished! The only fear is that a man will not resolve to do it, or will stop halfway. Therefore when one has made a good vow, one must possess a true faith, a courageous mind, a diligent mind, and a firm and enduring mind. Do not stop because you begrudge wealth; do not doubt because you fear men’s mockery; do not grow used to comfort and so fail to rouse yourself; do not let private desire entangle you and blunt your decisiveness; do not fear difficulty because a matter is great; do not neglect it because a good is small; do not make the excuse of being busy to shirk it; do not fail to save others in calamity out of concern for your own reputation. In short: avoid no suspicion, avoid no resentment, do not procrastinate, do not interrupt, do not be rash, do not seek reward, do not seek fame. Whenever you meet with any good deed at all, do it gladly and bring it to completion even at cost to yourself — this is truly accumulating virtue and piling up merit!

The Lady of Purple Emptiness said: ‘Once there was a Mr. Fu who loved to study the Way from childhood, and entered a stone chamber on Mount Jiao. After three years he suddenly met the Perfected of the Great Ultimate, who gave him a wooden drill and told him to use it to bore through a very great stone. And he further reminded him, saying: “If you bore through this great stone with a wooden drill, I will come to deliver you.” Mr. Fu drilled without cease, and went on drilling for forty-seven years, when the great stone suddenly was pierced through, and the Perfected of the Great Ultimate indeed came to deliver him.’ You should know that accumulating merit and piling up virtue does not consist in drilling stone; this is borrowed to illustrate that the only fear is that a man will not do it, or will stop halfway! So it is that ‘where there is a will, the matter is accomplished’ — Mr. Fu drilling the stone is a clear proof!

In the Song dynasty there was a governor of Zhenjiang named Ge Fan, who did several good deeds every day without a single day’s interruption for forty years. When someone asked him how, Ge Fan said: ‘I have no wonderful method; I merely do one or two things each day that benefit others.’ And he pointed with his finger at the footrest between the seats, saying: ‘If this footrest is placed crookedly, it will injure people’s feet; so I set it straight. When someone is thirsty, I offer him a cup of water. These are all things that benefit others! From prime minister down to beggar, anyone can do them; but one must certainly persevere and practice them for a long time before obtaining true benefit.’

Mr. Jiao was a man of the Eastern Capital. Because for three generations the Jiao family had lacked a legitimate son — that is, a son born of the principal wife — he traveled about on business everywhere, seeking out men of great understanding and asking them the causes and conditions of this. In time he met an old monk, who told him: ‘There are three reasons for having no son. The first is that neither your ancestors nor you yourself have accumulated merit and virtue. The second is that the years and destinies of husband and wife may offend against prohibitions. The third is that you do not take care of your essence and spirit, and your wife and concubines have the affliction of cold blood.’ Mr. Jiao said: ‘Accumulating merit and virtue, and the years and destinies of husband and wife, I can attend to; but as for the affliction of cold blood, what method can cure it?’ The old monk said: ‘That is not difficult. You need only first accumulate merit and virtue, and then regulate your body; after three years, come to Mount Wutai and I will transmit a special prescription to you.’ From then on Mr. Jiao constantly did acts of convenience and all kinds of hidden good, and after three years of thus accumulating merit and virtue he went straight to Mount Wutai to visit the old monk. He did not meet the old monk, but suddenly saw a novice who held a scroll in his hand and said to Mr. Jiao: ‘The old monk told me to pass on a message to you: after three full years of accumulating merit and virtue, go home, compound the medicine, and take it with utmost sincerity and reverence; you will surely have sons and grandsons of wealth and honor, born into your household according to your wish.’ Afterward Mr. Jiao indeed had a son, Jiao Yuanwai. But the son born to Jiao Yuanwai was unworthy; Jiao Yuanwai regretted that he himself had harmed his virtue to such a degree, and so went straight to Mount Wutai. He met the novice, who said: ‘The old monk told me to pass on a message to you: why need you come to ask? Only follow what your father Mr. Jiao did and earnestly accumulate merit and virtue, and then the sons and grandsons of your household — the foolish will naturally become worthy, and the poor will become rich.’ Jiao Yuanwai said: ‘That the poor afterward become rich is naturally their destiny; but foolishness is their nature from birth, and that cannot be changed. How can you say that the foolish can be made worthy?’ The novice said: ‘In former times Dou Yujun of Yanshan in the Later Zhou had five sons; when they were born they were all of poor health and imperfect in body. But afterward, because Dou Yanshan most sincerely accumulated merit and virtue, all five sons became well, and all of them passed the examinations — this is an absolutely certain fact!’ Hearing this, Jiao Yuanwai thanked the novice and returned home, where he strove desperately to accumulate merit and virtue, believing deeply without doubt; and twenty years later he not only had several sons, but every one of them was a noble son!

People today all know that Dou Yanshan had five sons who one after another became wealthy, honored, and illustrious. How would they know that when these five children were born they all suffered grave illness or deformity, and that it was only because Dou Yanshan desperately and most sincerely accumulated merit and practiced virtue that all five children were healed of their illnesses and became healthy, honored, and noble! From this it appears how easy it is for Heaven and man to respond to each other. May all who have a heart in this world firmly establish their faith in accumulating merit and virtue, and never be slack!
[Postscript]

In Liaofan’s Four Lessons for the Family written by Yuan Liaofan of the Ming dynasty, the chapter on accumulating good contains detailed explanations and examples of accumulating merit and virtue. Those who wish to understand and learn further should consult Elder Master Jingkong’s lectures on Liaofan’s Four Lessons, also titled The Way of Cultivating Blessings, Accumulating Virtue, and Creating Destiny; our society has also produced a radio drama version in Mandarin and Taiwanese for reference.
The good man who accumulates merit and piles up virtue not only loves his kin and is kind to the people; above all, his compassionate heart extends to all things!

Compassion is the benevolent heart, the root of all good. Compassion has two meanings: first, to relieve the poor and pull out suffering; second, to abstain from killing and further to release living creatures. This is the foundation of accumulating virtue and piling up merit, and the root of being a good person!

The Great Canon says: ‘If a man does not kill living beings, but cherishes the lives of animals and releases living creatures and gives food, he will obtain the retribution of long life.’ Nowadays when children in ordinary households play games, they often injure small creatures such as dragonflies, sparrows, and little birds; parents should sternly forbid this and not let children harm small animals. This not only harms the lives of those small creatures and damages the child’s blessings, but also fosters the child’s killer instinct; and when the child grows up, he will not understand benevolence and forgiveness in his dealings with others! As for the servants in a household, they often pour hot water on the ground, or when burning firewood and sweeping the floor they often injure small insects such as ants; this too should be prohibited! Whenever one sees any living being cast into a place of death — for example, moths flying into a lamp, insects falling into a net, sparrows and small birds beaten and wounded, ants trodden upon, fish and shrimp caught in nets, and so on — one should find convenient means to rescue and protect them and preserve their lives. These are the good deeds performed by people of great blessing and long life!

The Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows says: ‘If one can make living beings happy, then all the Tathagatas will be happy. Why is this? Because all Buddhas and Tathagatas take the great compassionate heart as their root. Because of living beings, the great compassion arises; because of the great compassion, the bodhi mind arises; and because the bodhi mind has arisen, one can accomplish perfect enlightenment. For living beings, what they love most is their own body and life; and for the Buddhas, living beings are what they love most! Therefore one who can save the lives of living beings can accomplish the vows of all the Buddhas.’ From this we can see that the thousands of words and ten thousand phrases of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas are nothing but teachings to save living beings from suffering; while the thousands of words and ten thousand phrases of demons and outer paths are nothing but teachings to eat the flesh of living beings! So we know that to urge others to release living creatures is to awaken their compassionate heart — this is the good cause of eternal joy! And to urge others to kill is to awaken their cruel heart — this is the root of suffering enmity and sin for kalpas without end! Therefore the very same words may create blessing or create calamity; how then can we speak without care?

Yang Bao of the Han dynasty, when he was nine years old, saw a yellow sparrow that had been bitten and wounded by a fierce owl and had fallen to the ground; and this wounded sparrow, fallen on the ground, was then surrounded and beset by many ants. Yang Bao quickly rescued the sparrow and placed it in a box to protect it, and fed it on yellow flowers; and when the sparrow’s wound was healed, Yang Bao set it free. One evening a boy dressed in yellow came to thank Yang Bao, and the yellow-robed boy said: ‘I am an envoy of the Queen Mother of the West. On my way to Penglai I passed through here and met with disaster; fortunately I was saved by you. To thank you for saving my life, I give you these four jade rings; they will enable your sons and grandsons, when they become officials, to reach the highest rank of the Three Excellencies, and their virtue and conduct will be as pure and white as these jade rings!’ Having said these words, the yellow-robed boy disappeared. Afterward Yang Bao had a son, Yang Zhen; Yang Zhen had Yang Bing; Yang Bing had Yang Ci; and Yang Ci had Yang Biao. Four generations in all, grandfather, father, son, and grandson, all rose in office to the Three Excellencies, and their virtue and conduct were exceedingly pure and clean — truly there was no one at that time who could compare with them!

Shen Wansan was a man of the Ming dynasty. Once he saw someone holding several hundred frogs and about to kill them all at once; Shen Wansan could not bear to see the frogs killed, and so he bought them all with money and released them into a pond, so that they could live and swim freely. One day Shen Wansan passed by the pond and saw a great crowd of frogs standing in a circle around a clay basin, croaking as if to say: ‘Shen Wansan, Shen Wansan, take the basin home with you!’ So Shen Wansan took the clay basin home and used it as a washbasin. Once, when he was washing his hands in the basin, a ring he wore on his hand fell into it; only the next morning did he notice and go to look for the ring in the basin. At that moment Shen Wansan suddenly found that the whole basin was full of rings. Shen Wansan was greatly astonished, and tried putting gold and silver into the basin, and the whole basin became full of gold and silver! So this clay basin was what is called a treasure-gathering basin! Thereupon Shen Wansan’s wealth became so great that it rivaled a nation’s, and no one could compare with him!

Chan Master Yongming Yanshou of the Song dynasty, whose secular surname was Wang, was a man of Danyang. At first he served as a tax official in Yuyao county; because he often bought fish to release them, his salary ran out, and as a last resort he misappropriated public funds. When a superior sent men to audit the treasury money, it was discovered that he had misappropriated several hundred thousand in public funds. According to the law of the time, Mr. Wang was sentenced to death; yet at the moment of execution his countenance did not change at all. And he said to his good friend, the execution supervisor of the time, Xu Zixin: ‘I have released hundreds of millions of living creatures; today I die without regret! Now with single-minded devotion I seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — is that not the greatest joy?’ So saying, he joined his palms in single-minded Buddha-recitation, not in the least afraid of death. Just as the headsman raised his steel blade and brought it down toward Mr. Wang’s neck, there was a clang, and the great blade broke into three pieces! The execution supervisor Xu Zixin at once wrote a memorial reporting the matter to King Qian Liu. This King Qian Liu was also a man of Buddhist faith and compassion, and when he saw the memorial he immediately ordered Mr. Wang’s crime pardoned, and restored his official post. But after Mr. Wang was released, he saw through the affairs of the world and left home to study the Buddha’s teaching, diligently and earnestly cultivating precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Once he dreamed that Avalokitesvara Bodhisattva poured sweet dew into his mouth, and thereafter his wisdom gradually opened. He wrote the Collection of the Common Return of Ten Thousand Goods in six fascicles, and long dwelt at Yongming Temple; afterward he was honored as the sixth patriarch of the Pure Land school. At the age of seventy-two he sat upright, joined his palms, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away. Later there was a monk who every day circumambulated and paid homage around Chan Master Yanshou’s stupa of relics. Someone asked him why, and the monk replied: ‘I am a renunciate of Fuzhou. Because some time ago I fell gravely ill, my soul was led by ghost-soldiers down to the underworld, and I saw in a corner of King Yama’s hall a hanging portrait. I saw King Yama himself bowing reverently in worship before the portrait. I was curious and asked the judge beside him: whose portrait is that? The judge answered: “It is a portrait of Chan Master Yongming Yanshou. Every person after death must pass through here; only Chan Master Yongming went straight to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and that in the highest grade of the highest rebirth. Therefore King Yama especially honors the Chan Master, and so bows in homage to his portrait.”’ From this we see that for compassionate release of living creatures and Buddha-recitation for rebirth in the West, even King Yama in the underworld bows to him in reverence!

Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty once wrote an essay on abstaining from killing to exhort the people of the world, saying: ‘Everyone cherishes his own life, and animals likewise fear death and cling to life; how then can we kill their bodies to satisfy the cravings of our mouths and bellies? When killing, one may slit open their bellies with a sharp knife, or pierce through their innards with a pointed blade; or strip off their skin, or scrape off their scales; or cut through their throats, or split open their shells; or boil turtles and eels alive in scalding water, or pickle crabs and shrimp raw in salt and wine. Pitiful! They suffer such great pain, and yet have nowhere to appeal! And this extreme suffering is truly past enduring! People who commit this sky-filling sin of slaughtering living beings thereby bind a blood-deep enmity of ten thousand ages with the creatures they have killed. Once impermanence arrives, they must at once fall into hell, and in hell undergo all kinds of cruel punishment: the cauldron of boiling water, the furnace of coals, the mountain of knives, the forest of swords. And after the suffering of hell is finished, they must still be reborn as animals to repay the debt of life for the living creatures they killed and ate. When the debt of life is repaid, they are reborn as human beings, but then they are sickly and die young. Therefore today I earnestly appeal to the people of the world, universally urging everyone to abstain from killing; and further, according to one’s own ability, to release living creatures and to recite the Buddha’s name for them. This will not only increase one’s own blessings and virtue, but will surely enable one to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss according to one’s vow, forever escaping the sea of suffering of the six realms of rebirth, and universally saving living beings — merit without measure!’
He who is a subject must do his utmost in loyalty; he who is a son or daughter must do his utmost in filial devotion.

That the subject exhausts his loyalty and the child exhausts his filial devotion is the constant rule of the principle of Heaven and the foundation of human relations. If a subject is not loyal, what hope can the ruler have in his subject? If a child is not filial, what hope can the parent have in his child? You should know that one who is disloyal and unfilial is not even the equal of beasts and birds — how can he be called a human being?

Though a man may cultivate to become an immortal, he must pass through long cultivation of accumulating merit and virtue; but one of utmost loyalty and great filial devotion, dying today, may be born into the heavens tomorrow. Ordinary people all know that loyalty and filial devotion are the great virtues of a subject; how would they know that loyalty and filial devotion are, even more, the fundamental cause of ascending to the heavens!

The filial son must first bring peace to the state, for only when the state is at peace can the family be at peace; and only when the family is at peace can the filial son practice filial devotion. Therefore when the ancients sought loyal ministers, they were certain to seek them at the gates of filial sons! And only if loyalty and filial devotion can both be fulfilled is one’s virtue as a human being at its highest; yet there are also cases in which loyalty and filial devotion cannot be fulfilled at the same time. Therefore they must be discussed separately, so that everyone may know how to do his utmost according to his own circumstances.

What is called loyalty means doing one’s utmost with no deception. Wherever human relationships obtain — for example, when a subordinate serves a superior, when a junior serves a senior, or in the dealings and conduct of friends of equal standing, in receiving people and handling affairs — one should do one’s utmost without deception. Yet the principle of loyalty belongs especially to the subject or subordinate; for in the relations of father and son, brothers, and husband and wife, everyone naturally knows that they should love and respect one another; whereas the relation of ruler and minister is joined by duty and righteousness. Ordinary people easily fall into carelessness in this place, and the reasons a subject is distracted and cannot be wholly loyal are no more than these five: his own person and family, his official position, power and influence, gratitude and grievance, and reputation. If he thinks of his own family and official position, he is mostly a mediocre man, and the bad influence he produces is still small; but thoughts of playing with power and manipulating influence mostly come from treacherous ministers, and then the welfare of the realm and the state is at stake; and these treacherous ministers in the end harm themselves as well — for example Li Linfu, Yang Guozhong, Qin Hui, and others. As for acting for the sake of gratitude, grievance, or reputation, even men whom the world calls gentlemen cannot avoid it; this is the cause of the calamity of factions and cliques from the Tang and Song dynasties onward!

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: ‘That the common people can dwell in peace and pursue their work and live out peaceful days depends entirely on the protection of the nation’s armies and police! Just think: if a place had no protection from the nation’s armies and police, then bandits and thieves would surely run wild, burning, killing, and plundering; would not the lives and property of the common people be in peril at every moment, uncertain from one morning to the next? So if one thinks of this, then even peddlers and runners are at every moment protected by the state! Therefore everyone should be loyal to the state according to his own station in life; how much more so for those who study and become officials and draw a salary from the state — if they do not understand this word “loyalty,” they should be truly ashamed!’

Wei Zheng, a famous minister of the Tang dynasty, had courage and strategy, and was skilled at undoing improper decisions made by the sovereign. Whether the matter was great or small, if the emperor was in the wrong, Wei Zheng would certainly remonstrate with him relentlessly and bitterly; even when the emperor was exceedingly angry, Wei Zheng still would not stop. Once, Emperor Taizong of the Tang obtained a fine sparrowhawk and was very fond of it, often perching it on his arm. Once, seeing Wei Zheng approach, and afraid that he would see it, he hastily hid the sparrowhawk in his bosom; Wei Zheng knew what was going on, and when reporting matters to Taizong he deliberately dragged out the time, so that the sparrowhawk suffocated to death in Emperor Taizong’s bosom. (This was because Wei Zheng did not want Emperor Taizong to lose his resolve through playing with things, harming the sovereign’s dignity; so he used this method to remonstrate.) Later, when Empress Wende passed away, Emperor Taizong could not stop thinking of her, and built a storeyed tower in the imperial garden so as to gaze at the empress’s tomb; and he invited Wei Zheng to ascend the tower with him and had Wei Zheng gaze at the empress’s tomb too. Wei Zheng looked carefully for a long while and then said: ‘Your Majesty! I am old and my eyes are dim; I cannot see it!’ Emperor Taizong pointed it out to him with his finger. Wei Zheng said: ‘I thought that if Your Majesty could gaze at the Xian Tomb of the ancestors as you gaze at the Zhao Tomb of the empress, then I would be able to see the empress’s Zhao Tomb!’ Hearing this, Emperor Taizong was moved to tears, and had the storeyed tower torn down, and no longer ascended it to gaze at the Zhao Tomb. Wei Zheng also urged Taizong to lay down arms and cultivate letters, to halt the development of military affairs and strengthen cultural education; thus China was at peace, and the peoples of the four quarters would naturally submit and pay allegiance, with no need to subdue them by force. Taizong adopted Wei Zheng’s counsel, and it indeed produced great effects. All of these are instances of Wei Zheng’s loyalty to the court. And Wei Zheng’s fifth-generation grandson, named Wei Mo, was exceedingly outstanding and rose to be prime minister.

Sima Wengong of the Song dynasty, as prime minister, was diligent in government and loved the people, and gave his life to the state; because of excessive toil he was already ill. At that time the pernicious laws established by Wang Anshi — the green sprouts loans, the exemption from service, and the garrison officers — had still not been abolished, and the state of Western Xia had not submitted to the Song. Sima Guang therefore sighed and said: ‘These four evils have not yet been removed; I shall not close my eyes in death!’ The guests who came to inquire after his illness, seeing him waste away day by day, brought up the precedent of Zhuge Kongming, who ‘ate little while his affairs were many, and so his life was not long,’ and reminded Sima Guang to take it as a warning. Sima Guang replied: ‘Life and death are fated; there is no need to worry.’ Instead he handled official business even more earnestly. Later his illness grew more and more grave, and his consciousness was no longer quite clear, yet he still never forgot the affairs of the court and the realm; even the words he spoke in dreams were all great matters of the court and the realm!

Emperor Gaozong of Wei told his assembled ministers: ‘One should treat one’s sovereign with the same reverence as one’s own father. When a father has a fault, a son will not write it out for the public to know in order to remonstrate with his father; rather he remonstrates with him privately where others cannot see, and the purpose of doing so is to avoid displaying the father’s fault! For example, when We had faults, Gao Yun always remonstrated with Us to Our face; sometimes he even made Us unable to bear it! But by remonstrating in this way, Gao Yun let Us know Our own faults while the world did not know them! Therefore Gao Yun was truly loyal to Us! And this wholehearted loyalty of Gao Yun’s was something that those who remonstrate in vehement ways could not achieve, and that those who remonstrate by satire and metaphor could not match! This is indeed a very good method of remonstrance.’

Su Bing, a minister of the Song dynasty, submitted a memorial to the court discussing the great affairs of state; not only was it not adopted by the court, but he was demoted to Raozhou. On the way to Raozhou, Su Bing passed through Luoyang and lodged in the home of his good friend Yin Tun, and complained to Yin Tun that he had been utterly loyal to the court and yet had come to such an end, banished to Raozhou. Hearing this, Yin Tun said to him: ‘When you submitted your memorial to the court, was your purpose to plan for the nation and the people’s livelihood, or to plan for your own name and position? If it was for the sake of the nation, then you should gladly go to take up your post in Raozhou. But if it was for the sake of your own advancement or retreat, then this punishment of being demoted to Raozhou is still a light one!’ Hearing this, Su Bing felt his heart set at ease, and no longer dared harbor any resentment toward the court.

Zhang Ke’an said: ‘If a scholar who has become an official harbors in his heart the wish to secure his own rank and fame and to win favor and please others, then it is impossible for him to accomplish a single thing that benefits the nation and the people!’ These are true words!

Guo Ziyi, the great general of the Tang dynasty, during the An Lushan rebellion recovered both the eastern and western capitals, and his merit surpassed that of the other generals. In the reign of Emperor Daizong, when the eunuchs held great power exclusively, Guo Ziyi was left idle for a long time and his subordinates scattered. Suddenly at this time the Tibetans rebelled and marched straight against the capital; the capital was shaken, and the emperor hastily led his civil and military officials to Shanzhou for refuge. Great generals such as Li Guangbi, all because they detested the eunuchs’ monopoly of power, kept their troops to themselves and were unwilling to go to Shanzhou to rescue the emperor. Only Guo Ziyi alone recruited twenty cavalrymen and at once set out for Shanzhou to rescue the emperor. On the way he gathered other generals as well, beating war drums and displaying banners; and he lit fires in many places, so that the Tibetans grew suspicious and, in fear, all fled. Later the Tibetans again joined with the Uyghurs, and with an army of several hundred thousand attacked the Tang. Most of the Tang generals could not arrive in time to protect the capital; only Guo Ziyi alone rode out to persuade the Uyghurs to withdraw, and further routed the Tibetan army. Though Guo Ziyi was a great general with powerful forces under his command, the eunuchs Cheng Yuanzhen and Yu Chao’en slandered and defamed him in every way before the emperor. But whenever a single edict from the emperor summoned him to the capital for audience, Guo Ziyi would set out for the capital at once upon the edict’s arrival to have audience with the emperor; therefore he greatly enjoyed the emperor’s trust, and all the slander and defamation against him could not shake the emperor’s trust in him. Guo Ziyi was later enfeoffed by the emperor as Prince of Fenyang, and his eight sons and seven sons-in-law all rose to high office; and Guo Ziyi’s descendants were all exceedingly illustrious, noble, and prosperous beyond compare!

We see that from ancient times to the present, the examples of subjects who obtained good retribution because of their loyalty are truly too numerous to count! As for those subjects who stood firm in great matters of principle, gave their lives when they saw danger, and even killed themselves to complete their benevolence — in the eyes of ordinary people they truly bore eternal regret, and it seems that Heaven’s recompense to them was so different! You should know that these loyal ministers who died for their country enjoyed the great fame of their age while alive, and after death receive the bowing worship of ten thousand people. So Heaven’s recompense to them is truly a hundred times higher than that given to those who enjoy wealth, honor, peace, and pleasure! And as for officials disloyal to the state who bring harm to the common people, the severity of Heaven’s retribution upon them need not even be mentioned! Let us not speak now of the retribution of loyalty or disloyalty; look only at those mediocre officials whose hearts are not bound to the common people of the realm — not one of them comes to a good end either! Thus it is evident that ‘your stipend and your salary are the fat and the marrow of the people’; therefore public servants absolutely must not be untrue to this word “loyalty”!

Mr. Yan Guangzhong, discussing filial devotion, said: ‘Where in the world is there a man who is not filial? Though there are unfilial men, if you call one of them filial, he is delighted to hear it; if you say he is unfilial, he is angry and ashamed to hear it; and before others he will still put on a show of propriety and save face, not daring to be as unrestrained as he is in private. This too shows that his innate moral knowledge is not extinguished; so if only one extends this innate moral knowledge, it is the sprout of great filial devotion. But if one still does not earnestly reflect and change this evil habit, then one remains unfilial as before! In this matter, if one analyzes clearly and understands distinctly, then a father will know how to educate his children, and a child will know how to restrain himself; just as in attacking bandits, one must know where the bandits are, and then the pacification of the bandit trouble may be expected in a matter of days!’
He also said: there are four reasons why small unfilialness comes to be formed.

The first is pampering and favoritism. Parents dote too much on their children: for example, they constantly indulge the child’s temperament, so that if anything goes slightly against his wishes he cannot bear it. They constantly let him off lightly and let him be at ease and enjoy himself, so that when he is told to do the labor of serving his parents he is not used to it. When the child has some slight fault before others, the father cannot bear to reprove him, and the child then dares to offend his father. The father praises the child’s literary learning, conduct, talents, and abilities, fearing only that they may not be above his own; while the child insists that the father’s literary learning, conduct, and abilities be below his own. Having accumulated these habits of arrogance and self-indulgence, he cannot show them off before others, but only before his parents; and so he comes truly to think that old and experienced people have neither knowledge nor experience!

The second is habit. When the child’s speech has grown crude by habit, he dares to contradict his parents; when his behavior has grown offhand by habit, he dares to disregard propriety and act as he pleases. When the parents have grown used to giving him the sweet and keeping the little for themselves, the child then does not remember the kindness of his parents in leaving the delicacies for him to eat; when the parents have grown used to bearing illness and enduring its pain, the child then no longer asks after his parents’ aches and itches.

The third is delight in license. When the child sees his own generation, he cannot contain his high spirits; when he faces his parents, he feels there is no pleasure in it. Entering his wife’s chamber, he displays a thousand charming airs; walking into the tall hall, he feels sullen and unhappy, and even dares to say openly that father and brothers are commonplace creatures whom he does not like to meet. How then could there remain in his heart any thought of filial devotion and fraternal respect?

The fourth is forgetting kindness and remembering grievances. As the common saying goes: ‘Kindness long accustomed is the more forgotten; resentment long accustomed is the more accumulated.’ This too is human nature! Thus the kindness of one meal offered to another is easily remembered by him; but if the hospitality becomes a long habit, then disdain and resentment will arise. One act of charity makes another grateful; but if the relief is constant, then comparisons of how much or how little will arise. A single meeting makes people feel especially close; but repeated meetings breed speculation and suspicion. How much more so with parents and brothers, whose love one is born into and grows used to, so that one takes the affection of parents and brothers as something that certainly will not change, and does not even know the great kindness of one’s parents before one’s eyes — much less can one think of the hardship of one’s mother’s pregnancy and rearing, or of her fear and anxiety when one was ill? Therefore human feelings are sometimes utterly inverted and utterly perverse, and one does not even notice it. Children often behave thus toward their parents; hence there are very few parents who receive resentment instead of gratitude!

The several kinds described above are all habitual feelings of human beings; yet sons and daughters are not without their true nature — it is only that after long accumulation of habit they do not know where the fault lies. Therefore one should urgently awaken, correct and govern oneself early, and reflect constantly. Do not think that because your parents’ hearts are kind they will naturally forgive you; do not think that because the ways of the world are shallow you are still better than others. You should know that small unfilialness, accumulated over long time, will become great unfilialness!
He also said: there are likewise four reasons why great unfilialness comes to be formed.

The first is private wealth. Money that comes into my hands is mine; and the money in my parents’ hands I likewise regard as money that is mine. When my own money is sufficient, I forget my parents; and when my money is insufficient, I covet my parents’ money. When parents cannot support themselves and must rely on their children to support them, then I resent my parents; and there have even occurred cases of a single father and an only son killing each other over money, and of brothers shifting responsibility to one another and abandoning their parents without support! Do I not know from whose body my own body came? From whom did my own money come? Since I brought not a single coin into the world with me, and from infancy to now have never lacked for anything in my life, whose help was that? Yet now, merely to earn a few more coins for myself, I want to haggle with my parents!

The second is clinging to wife and children. To love wife and children and be unfilial to parents is a grave matter. When there are fine foods and money, one wants to please one’s wife and pamper one’s children; when a fine season and beautiful scene comes, one wants to embrace wife and children, and the thought of making one’s parents happy grows fainter and fainter. One does not think: my children are my children, but whose child am I? If my parents raised me, and I do not care for my parents, then what use is it that I raise children? That husband and wife are harmonious is indeed a joy of the household; but when I was an infant waiting to be fed, not yet knowing the difference between filth and cleanliness, how could I have understood the love of wife and children? And how could a wife at that time have cared for and raised me? When parents see their son grown to manhood and taking a wife, their joy knows no bounds; how then can the arrival of a wife cause the parents to lose their son?

The third is whoring and dissipation. The fire of desire in the heart is at its blazing height, and the other party’s enticement is exceedingly powerful; at such a time, even though there be one in the house who leans at the gate in sorrow, he cannot understand it! Whoring and dissipation waste money extravagantly, so that mother-in-law and daughter-in-law quarrel over it, and even fiercely blame each other, and he cannot distinguish between them! His wife holds the child and lies awake all night because her husband is abroad whoring, and even the wind and rain outside weep for her; his aged parents’ temples are white, yet no one is at their knees to gladden them; and even the meager material support they receive is endangered by their son’s whoring. Alas! When whoring and dissipating, how long can the mad excitement last? And yet he has the heart to make those dearest to him so sorrowful!

The fourth is contention and jealousy. Since even the selfless Heaven and earth leave men feeling that something is wanting, how could the feelings of parents toward their children fail to be partial? And so children contend with one another for their parents’ favor: brothers may be uneven in their jealousies, sisters may haggle over the finest details; they slander and poison one another, and the family fortunes decline thereby; and as anger, hatred, joy, and displeasure accumulate, the filial heart weakens thereby. These four conditions are common human feelings, and even filial sons can hardly avoid them; yet their corrupting influence ends in great unfilialness!

Han Weigong (Han Qi) of the Song dynasty said: ‘That parents are kind and children filial is an ordinary matter and not worth mentioning; only when parents are unkind and the child does not fail in filial devotion is what has made the great Shun praised through the ages.’ A child in the situation of having unkind parents must not harbor the least spark of anger in his heart; he must serve his parents with redoubled care compared to ordinary children. Parents of kind heart will naturally be moved and turn to pity their child; but parents without kindness, since they cannot be transformed, must all the more not be offended. One can only fulfill one’s own duty as a child, and not let oneself fall into the great sin of rebellious unfilialness. If one merely sees one’s parents’ faults and lets one’s heart be filled with resentment, unable to dispel it and unable to be free of it, then there will surely come a time when it can no longer be held in check; this is what is meant by failing to remove the tiny root, until at last it bursts its banks and becomes a flood. I fear that by that time, the fault of blaming one’s parents for being unkind is light, while the great sin of rebellious unfilialness cannot be escaped!

Mr. Luo once said: ‘In serving his parents, a filial son must not let his parents feel chilled; must not cause his parents to give rise to affliction; must not let his parents feel alarm or dread; must not cause his parents to give rise to sorrow and gloom; must not let his parents have feelings they cannot speak of; must not let his parents have feelings of shame and regret.’

Mr. Tang’s Song of Parental Kindness says:

Ere yet I speak, my tears begin to fall —
How shall I repay the love that gave me all?
These are heartbreak words I hardly dare to say;
Heartbreak words I tell to all today.

Only the bearing of a child is pain and dread,
A hundred trials through which she must be led.
Say not that birth knows neither ill nor good;
In one brief breath she stands where death has stood.

Within her womb the pain grows sharp and sore;
She bids them loosen her clothing more and more.
Through a thousand births and deaths no count can be —
On Heaven and the gods alone her trust must be.

The child is born: blood rushes to her heart;
Her teeth are clenched, her eyes roll back and start.
Only when the afterbirth is cut away,
And three more dawns have passed, is he a man of clay.

His filth and water soil her all day long;
The stench and foulness are past bearing strong.
Yet not a trace of loathing in her breast:
She washes, changes, toiling without rest.

She hears the baby utter one small cry,
And turns to lift him up without delay.
Think: in his year and half, did she once lie
And sleep her fill until the break of day?

She hears her child has caught the smallpox sore;
At once her eyes turn yellow with her fright.
From the day the rash came out and nothing more,
Did she once taste rice-broth from morn to night?

She kowtows low and burns a stick of incense,
Calling the Pox Goddess with every breath.
Could she but win the Goddess’s response,
She would not shrink from broken skull and death.

Thank heaven, the child has reached two years and more,
And walks alone beside the bench and door.
She fears he will fall and break his face and head —
Her heart is drawn and tied, her peace is fled.

The child is born with temper crooked and wild;
She lets him have his way in everything.
How then do parents dote upon the child,
And call him good, and of his goodness sing?

His hair now hangs down to his shoulders long;
In a blink, a grown man before them stands.
It cuts the parents’ hearts to let him go —
He cannot stay forever in their hands.

Though he has won a little field and plot,
With fear and toil unnumbered for his lot;
If not for sons and daughters all his care,
How few the coppers he would spend or share!

Mother looks at father, father looks at mother;
Why are their two faces sallow all day long?
Because their sons and daughters must be wed —
They sit with anxious brows in one room’s throng.

Each inch and thread is kindness through and through;
Who can portray one half a hair of it?
Even the poem Liao E, for all it knew,
Could render but six or seven parts of it.

Mr. Jin Shaosong said: ‘By now the corruption of funeral rites has reached its extreme. Modern people in everything think that the funeral rites of the ancients were incorrect; and nowadays there are even those who, within the forty-nine days of mourning, hurry to complete a marriage — this is especially absurd and outrageous! When the gentlemen of ancient times observed mourning for their parents, they did not find good food sweet, nor music joyful; in their daily life and conduct they still grieved over their parents’ passing, and so it was for three full years. Yet now there are actually people who, ignoring conscience and defying the principle of Heaven, instead marry within the forty-nine days, setting aside mourning for their parents to pursue the pleasure between husband and wife. If a son or daughter does this, it is simply great unfilialness! And if parents teach their children to do so, they are teaching their children great unfilialness! Moreover, to perform an auspicious affair in the midst of mourning is inauspicious for both husband and wife. Who first began this custom, no one knows, but by today it has become an accepted practice. Even families of poetry and propriety have had such things happen among them; they are truly sinners against the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, and this corrupt custom should be earnestly and thoroughly forbidden!’

Mr. Shen Longjiang said: ‘For a child in serving his parents, there is no greater matter than seeing them to their grave. If one cannot exhaust his heart even in this great matter of seeing his parents off, then how could he exhaust his heart in any other matter? There are those who, because the family has many brothers, shirk responsibility upon one another, and so handle the parents’ funeral in a hasty manner, leading to remorse and regret in later days.
